The fixed point is also found in normalized factorial cumulant behavior for at least fourth-order cumulants and is mapped into the QCD, resulting in a similar fixed point in energy dependence along different freeze-out curves in QCD.

A characterization of finite-dimensional commuting squares of C*-algebras, resulting in hyperfinite type II_1 subfactors of finite index and depth, is provided, utilizing Morita equivalent unitary fusion categories. We extend a prior investigation by N. Sato, generalizing his findings to encompass the broader context of such squares. Additionally, we establish a characterization for such squares yielding a given type II_1 subfactor, and this analysis contributes to a broader understanding of 4-tensors related to matrix product operators in 2-dimensional topological systems.

In this work, we introduce a novel meta-learning framework centered on ODE neural networks, which acquires an understanding of gradients. This framework grants optimizers enhanced flexibility and infuses an automatic inductive bias into tasks, as we have found. Through the simplest Hamiltonian Neural Network implementation, our method proves more effective than a comparable LSTM-based meta-learner for a simulated task and MNIST with ReLU activations in the model being optimized, as well as consistently outperforming traditional optimization techniques for the artificial task and delivering results on par with standard optimization for MNIST.

Simply enhancing a machine learning model's accuracy is not sufficient, as we must also focus on increasing its interpretability and reliability. This consideration is particularly important for multi-agent environments, where a single human user supervises several models that interact and alter one another. In this study, we propose a novel, original method that combines increase in trustworthiness from both human and non-human sources. This is achieved through two key mechanisms: allowing a human to modify a single label to increase trust from a human source, and utilizing a human to collect high-quality training data. This is implemented as a multi-agent system where several Humans in the Loop learning agents simultaneously apply these mechanisms to several target classifiers. In this setup, the model portions modified by non-human sources are compensated for by having the human collect data, thus reducing the human's involvement. We evaluate the effectiveness of this system through a human trial and by simulating human behavior, demonstrating that it outperforms a single-source approach by enabling faster growth in model trust.

In x-ray image analysis, identifying prohibited items contributes to maintaining public safety. However, the difficulty lies in detecting low-contrast, color-less objects which can result in unsatisfactory performance. Until now, there have been limited studies in this field due to the absence of high-quality specialized datasets. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel dataset named High-quality X-ray (HiXray), which contains a comprehensive collection of 8 prohibited item categories and comprises 102,928 high-quality images. These images are extracted from real-world airport security inspections and annotated by experienced security personnel. Moreover, we propose a Lateral Inhibition Module (LIM) that mimics human ability to ignore low-quality areas and focus on bright colors and distinct boundaries to enhance prohibited items detection. Experimental results demonstrate that the HiXray dataset and LIM are effective in improving the performance of various prohibited items detection models, outperforming state-of-the-art methods both quantitatively and qualitatively.

A newly defined polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is established for links in a thickened torus. A proof is provided that these polynomials are invariants of such links, and it is demonstrated that they reduce to the standard colored Jones polynomials when a specific scoring function is applied to links defined in the torus. Additionally, the expectation values of these polynomials are found to conform to the volume conjecture, as proposed by Fauser and Kuperberg.

The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies being developed to combine structured knowledge for enhanced performance.  Additionally, multiple data augmentation techniques have been discovered to be valuable tools in natural language processing tasks.  Building on prior work, we introduce a novel technique called CA, a method that integrates context-gloss knowledge to refine WSD.  Experimental evaluation of our approach was conducted on the MultiNLI dataset, where CA was shown to outperform a baseline technique in several benchmarks, with notable improvements observed in low-frequency occurrences.  These results indicate that context-gloss knowledge is a valuable resource for the effective disambiguation of words.

This study formulates a genuine integral expression of the reciprocal gamma function in terms of a modified hypersingular integral. It also proves the connection to the traditional complex representation, in addition to obtaining a modified complex representation following the standard Hankel path.

The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an energy level of 5.02 TeV. The analysis involved 126 proton-lead interactions and considered a variety of unusual signatures, specifically focusing on one involving neutral and charged electrons or muons. The top quark production findings were compared to predictions based on the standard model of particle physics. Relative to proton-proton predictions normalized by the number of participating nuclei, the data indicated a lower rate of top quark production in certain energy ranges. These discrepancies may be influenced by the specific type of nuclear interaction occurring, such as the fusion of gluons within the nucleus. Notably, the current data set is not large enough to separately analyze the interaction dynamics in proton-lead data.

This study focuses on key elements in cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, specifically schema linking and value filling. A novel auxiliary task is proposed to enhance text-to-column mapping learning, utilizing a multi-task framework. To address value filling challenges, a novel beginning character generation approach is introduced. Empirical findings indicate significant improvements, achieving state-of-the-art results on the Spider dataset with a exact match rate of 69.4%.

This paper delves into the utilization of differential privacy within the framework of graph-based data. It outlines the DP formulations relevant to publishing graphs, statistical analysis associated with graphs, and machine learning on graph-based data. Despite rapid advancements in this field, a significant portion of research is centered around specific applications and methods. A key challenge in working with graph data is that standard techniques often fail to adequately capture the complex interconnections and interdependencies inherent in such datasets. While research on DP-based machine learning on graph data is in its nascent stages, a key question remains whether such approaches can be considered reliable. A key objective of this paper is to highlight the limitations of applying DP to graph-based data and explore the underlying reasons for these constraints.

The vast amount of images, data, and resources that Euclid will generate positions the consortium to create comprehensive legacy databases of outstanding quality, encompassing high-resolution near-infrared spectroscopy with significant implications for the study of galaxies. These proceedings outline the promising opportunities and scientific breakthroughs Euclid will achieve in the areas of galaxy and AGN development, the evolution of the cosmos, investigations of the Milky Way, and various other celestial bodies and phenomena.

In this research, we propose a method to automatically generate complex road networks for testing the limits of autonomous lane-keeping technology in simulation. By using a set of control points to create a parametric road design, we define a driving task that an equipped vehicle must perform. Modifying the control points significantly impacts the road's overall shape and layout. Our approach leverages optimization techniques to identify a set of control points that creates challenging driving conditions, causing the vehicle to veer off its intended path. We validated our method with three distinct search configurations, focusing on balancing testing speed and practicality for simulated evaluations of autonomous lane-keeping systems.

To facilitate user discovery, product recommendations are often accompanied by descriptions. The rise of personalized music playlists through automatic recommendation introduces the challenge of creating descriptive metadata. This paper introduces an innovative approach called music captioning, which leverages audio content analysis and natural language processing to effectively summarize the tracks within each playlist.

Researchers have successfully used hydrodynamic theories to simulate complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems, and in this work, we've developed a novel stochastic hydrodynamic approach for describing interacting Bose gases within a specific phase-space framework. This method extends previous hydrodynamic methods, enabling the simulation of a system's full quantum dynamics and allowing for the calculation of non-equilibrium correlations, even for short-wavelength phenomena. Building upon this description, we derived a linearized hydrodynamic model for small non-equilibrium perturbations and found that it replicates key features of precise calculations based on the Bogoliubov theory, including correct dispersion relations. Furthermore, we applied our method to an equally distributed non-equilibrium scenario and found that it can efficiently simulate the system's long-term relaxation behavior.

Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. A key challenge lies in existing boundary matching methods that exhaustively evaluate all possible combinations of start and end times, rather than directly acting on the concept of a single action. In response to this issue, we propose DCAN, a solution that conceptually captures the essence of one action by aggregating context information from both preceding and following frames. Specifically, we extract contextual information from adjacent frames at frequent time intervals throughout the action's duration, and then integrate this bi-directional context to rank the best potential boundaries. Our experiments conducted on two widely used benchmark datasets demonstrate significant improvements in boundary F1 scores compared to state-of-the-art methods on the DAVo dataset and MSRA-IOA dataset.

The long-lived palm tree modes (PTM) found in the JET tokamak's edge plasma remain somewhat enigmatic despite significant computational resources devoted to understanding them. A distinctive feature of these modes is their type-E ripple along the field lines, which sets them apart from other localized modes. A theoretical model combining a 5D drift-cyclotron kinetic model with a 1D nonlinear mode code has been developed to better grasp the PTMs. It is revealed that a PTM sustains a ripple well within the edge plasma and that a 5D solution is fundamentally required to accurately capture this behavior. The model's predictions are aligned with JET experiments and demonstrate that a PTM distinguishes itself by a ripple well-formed edge plasma structure.

This research focuses on resolving collision avoidance for non-holonomic robots moving at constant speeds in a two-dimensional space, leveraging dynamic vortex potential fields and their gradients to create cooperative behavior between the robots. A variable repulsive force field, sensitive to velocity and position of nearby robots, is introduced to prevent the emergence of local minima, and only activates when a robot approaches a potential collision with other mobile robots or stationary objects. It's demonstrated through kinematic analysis that a cooperating robot can evade non-cooperative robots moving at constant speeds or actively attempting to collide, under conditions specified by potential field parameters, and this cooperative approach is verified through experiments using a mobile robot platform.

Given an independent and identically distributed sequence of letters, a significant subexponential large deviation principle is established for the probability of rare events, such as waiting times for rare words, and their first occurrence distribution. This principle enables an investigation into the distribution of first occurrence lengths for rare words in an independent and identically distributed sequence of words. 

However, our study extends this principle to dependent letter sequences, specifically those with an absolute summability property for their mixing coefficients. We adapt the dependent independent letter sequences to analyze rare words, their waiting times, and their first occurrence distribution. 

Furthermore, we modify the significant subexponential large deviation principle to apply to this dependent sequence of words. This modified principle leads to distinct exponential decay rates for rare words and their waiting times, as well as their first occurrence distribution. In contrast, our first occurrence distribution returns to its original form for rare letters, but exhibits distinct behavior for rare words with overlapping patterns, exhibiting exponential decay.

Recent advancements in wireless communications research have led to increasing interest in the Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) technology.  This paper investigates the potential of IRS systems to improve the performance of radar platforms, specifically in terms of target parameter estimation.  We explore the underlying mechanisms of IRS-assisted radar platforms, and analyze how factors such as the presence of line-of-sight (LOS) connections and the variability of target parameters can be leveraged to enhance target estimation.  Our investigation focuses on the estimation of target direction and range, and we propose novel configurations for radar systems that utilize IRS systems to improve the estimation of these parameters.  We assess the performance of these configurations through both simulation and experimental means.  Our results demonstrate that radar systems aided by IRS platforms can significantly outperform traditional line-ray radar systems in terms of target parameter estimation accuracy.

Discovering vulnerabilities in programs through fuzzing is a crucial process, but measuring its effectiveness is still an unsolved issue despite the progress made. A widely accepted evaluation standard in software testing is mutation analysis, assessing the ability to detect artificial faults, and it encompasses a variety of measures that evaluate the sensitivity of test generation approaches to the difficulty of injected faults. However, the suitability of these strategies for comparing fuzzers remains unclear, primarily due to the fact that tests are not inserted randomly and the control and modification of program behavior during the execution of fuzzing remains limited. A previous study attempted to introduce the concept of attributing reachability to states that are reached during fuzzing, but it also included states that are reached only due to test generation limitations rather than the programmer's control. This study delves into the concepts of reachability in relation to fuzzing and it also presents tailored versions of mutation operators enabling a more precise evaluation of fuzzer performance. A total of 1,800 mutations were generated for three well-known fuzzing targets, resulting in findings that suggest the inclusion of reachability in relation to reachability in a more accurate evaluation of fuzzer performance, surpassing the alternative of flatly combining all reached states. Furthermore, this study finds that controlled modification of state behavior during fuzzing is feasible, paving the way for the development of a new framework that will serve as a robust evaluation standard for comparing the efficacy of fuzzers.

Following the success of transfer learning with pre-trained models in
deep learning, there has been a significant interest in adapting CL models to
build upon previously learned tasks. However, a deep understanding of CL
algorithms remains elusive. A primary objective of this research is to address
this gap by exploring the fundamental CL scenarios using pre-trained models. We
have designed a straightforward yet effective baseline algorithm that achieves
comparable results to more complicated CL approaches. Our Baseline exhibits
comparable performance to various Backward-Incompatible and Forward-Compliant
CL algorithms. Notably, our Baseline yields superior results in our experiments
when comparing with BICA-CL and LC-CL variants. A deeper analysis of our
Baseline reveals that it can achieve even better outcomes with alternative
implementations. Moreover, our Baseline can surpass even the performance of
state-of-the-art pre-trained models through curriculum-based model averaging.
A series of analyses including visualizations support these findings and provide
a framework for a more informed understanding of CL algorithms.

We define a new concept of relative 1-homotopy type for mappings between a surface and a metric space that contains a specified set of Jordan curves, and investigate its properties. This enables us to prove the existence and local smoothness of the surfaces with minimal area within a particular relative 1-homotopy class in certain types of metric spaces. Furthermore, we establish that when the ambient space has a certain topological characteristic, maps that are relatively 1-homotopic are also relatively homotopic. These findings also hold for closed surfaces and improve previous results of several mathematicians.

This final installment concludes our comprehensive study of the solution behavior for a specific type of parabolic equation on the real line. This particular equation takes a general form, involving a nonlinear diffusion term and an external force. We examined solutions under circumstances where the initial data can be divided into two distinct, well-separated components, and investigated how solutions develop over both short and long time periods. When the external force remains confined, we discovered that solutions eventually take on a specific form, closely related to the larger of the two initial components. However, when the external force is not decaying, we found that the eventual solution behavior takes on a diverse set of outcomes. These outcomes depend on the general form of the equation and the characteristics of the external force.

Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus with a low-spin structure have provided significant insights: combining data from four experiments allowed researchers to identify several 0+ and 2+ excited states below 4.5 MeV, and characterize their properties. Using a Monte Carlo shell model, scientists were able to explain the findings and uncover a surprisingly intricate pattern of shapes existing together, where a high-energy prolate 0+ state at 3463 keV, and a collective 2+ state just above it, could be explained by the balance between the shell model and tensor forces, bringing them to the same energy level.

Approximately ten years since its origin, the field of algorithms for computing approximate correlated equilibria in games has made substantial progress on a variety of game types including convex payoffs in Lipschitz games, where the payoffs change at a limited rate in a correlated random signals. Current algorithms for determining O(log^3 n)-approximate correlated equilibria in such games achieve this by finding distributions over pure strategies in a game of size n. We introduce a fundamental limit for this problem, demonstrating that any classical algorithm requires at best determining Omega(n)-approximate correlated equilibria in such games when given limited information about the game. Our lower bound also applies to randomized queries that are limited in the amount of information they gain about the game.

Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the particular KV implementation. This sensitivity underscores the need for performance evaluation methods that are more reliable and less prone to fluctuation. This paper suggests modifying the standard approach by conducting CV over K distinct justice-knowledge pairs, from which the most consistently performing model is chosen. Our findings suggest that this J-K approach yields performance enhancements of up to 10% and reduces optimal parameter variation by a similar margin.

Deep learning's success has been attributed to innovative architecture and knowledge. This paper explores a new class of knowledge-enhanced learning models called teacher-student architectures. Initially, these models were developed by integrating pre-defined components into learning frameworks, but a more versatile approach has since been created, where both the teacher and student components are artificial intelligence systems that collaborate to transfer knowledge and generate new insights. This collaborative process is governed by a set of optimization principles that determine the architecture's efficiency. Due to the growing complexity of these systems, a visual overview and systematic analysis of various teacher-student architectures is necessary to guide their future evolution.

We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in graphical models, which serves as a foundation for a variety of computational tasks. Our concise model then leverages this framework, specifically using deterministic finite state automata within a variable elimination approach known as Bucket Elimination. We dub this variant FABE, which we found significantly enhances Bucket Elimination by substantially reducing the computational time and memory usage. Our FABE approach compares favourably to the current state of the art methods, particularly recursive best-first and structured message passing for the most probable explanation, as well as CPLEX, GUROBI and toulbar2 for constrained optimisation, by achieving a 5 orders of magnitude improvement in our experiments.

We investigated the absorption of a single, monochromatic light beam at 689 nm as it passes through a cloud of ultracold $^{88}$Sr atoms. Due to the interaction, the absorption pattern deviates significantly, taking on an asymmetric shape as a result of a shift in frequency that is equivalent in magnitude to the natural width of a specific atomic transition in strontium. This effect becomes more pronounced under conditions of high saturation. Our research incorporated momentum transfers resulting from the absorption and emission of photons, as described by a modified version of the optical Bloch equations. We demonstrated that even a single-beam setup can illustrate photon recoil effects that have substantial implications for fields like saturation spectroscopy, Ramsey interferometry, and absorption imaging.

When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a transition from fluid-like behavior to a state of infinite viscosity. Researchers are exploring various theories to understand this phenomenon's underlying mechanisms, including models that posit the formation of a percolating jammed structure within the fluid, which suddenly fails at a critical stress threshold. By analyzing three distinct mixtures experiencing shear thickening, we subjected them to sonication for an extended period, and observed a shift in their response, marked by a stress-induced peak in the sonication volume. Notably, the stress at which this peak occurs when sonicated, rather than the yield stress, shows a universal relationship with the shear thickening transition, in contrast to the stress-induced peak yield stress, which shows only a loose correlation with the shear thickening transition, displaying disparate exponents.

Recently introduced is a higher rank algebra known as the Racah algebra $R(n)$. A special variant, termed the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$, is then defined as a quotient of the Racah algebra by its central elements. It is then demonstrated that this $sR(n)$ algebra is equivalent to the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ through application of classical invariant theory, specifically with respect to a natural action of the symmetric group $S_n$ on the polynomial algebra with $n$ second degree variables. Consequently, its Hilbert-Poincar\'e series can comprehensively studied and an expression provided for its coefficients in terms of the Littlewood-Richardson coefficients.

Our study shows that in a bilayer Heisenberg antiferromagnet, low-lying triplon
excitations may offer a suitable path to achieving magnetic analogs of twisted
superfluid and supersolid phases previously found in ultracold atomic condensates
trapped in optical lattices. Employing a cluster Gutzwiller mean-field theory,
we prove that Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions are responsible for stabilizing
these phases within a magnetic framework, in contrast to the tile-like lattice
necessary in the case of atomic systems. Moreover, we reveal that the twisted
superfluid and supersolid phases can be associated with long-range magnetic
order patterns exhibiting Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya spiral and supersolid symmetries
respectively. Through Monte Carlo simulations, we further establish that
twisted supersolid ferromagnetic order emerges from a linear combination of
Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya spiral spin order and Néel spiral spin order, thereby
indicating the potential for twisted supersolid ferromagnetism to manifest as a
robust and experimentally verifiable phenomenon, such as through Heisenberg
exchange interactions between adjacent layers in cuprate cupolates.

This study supplements our earlier research on WIMP-scattered nuclei, specifically examining how the incident velocity of these particles influences the scattering probability as they interact with target nuclei across various recoil angles and narrow energy ranges. Our simulation reveals that not only do the incident velocity characteristics of halo WIMPs play a crucial role, but so does the angle of the recoil itself, resulting in an irregular correlation of the two in specific energy ranges. Consequently, attempting to infer the 1-dimensional velocity distribution within these ranges directly from the overall WIMP halo velocities may not provide a complete or accurate understanding, which would ultimately distort our calculations of the associated scattering event rates in those particular ranges.

An area where Web search personalisation's effect on professional work has been little studied is that of professional journalists who depend on Google's Web search for up-to-date news. A key concern regarding this topic is whether this happens to be a unique experience. To examine this, we journalists utilized Google's Web search during a focus group, utilizing both unmodified and naturally modified search results. Participants' opinions were gathered through subjective measures and observed behaviors. The findings revealed that the naturally modified search results led to distinct differences in the topics that were identified as most relevant to a given topic, compared to the unmodified search results. Notably, these variations were not random but rather correlated with participants' demographics and prior knowledge, confirming the influence of Web search personalisation on the opinions of professional journalists who rely on Google's Web search for news.

We are suggesting the establishment of a state-of-the-art muon-proton and muon-nucleus collider that operates at the TeV level, capable of delivering highly accurate measurements in deep inelastic scattering in new areas, while also offering a comprehensive research agenda in particle and nuclear physics. By doing so, we believe it could either drive the advancement or make use of existing particle accelerators, specifically taking advantage of established infrastructure if constructed at places like Brookhaven National Laboratory, Fermilab, or CERN. In this concept, we outline various design parameters for several collider configurations and evaluate potential for scientific discoveries with studies on deep inelastic scattering processes, Higgs boson and vector boson production, top quark creation, and heavy beyond-Standard Model particle creation. Additionally, considerations for detector designs and potential construction timelines are also discussed.

A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI images for accurate drug targeting and treatment planning. This method employs a rapid, free-breathing turbo spin-echo sequence, which is then compared to a slower, breath-hold slice-by-spin-echo reference sequence in a phantom study. A multi-channel MRI scanner, equipped with respiratory bellows and real-time distortion correction, facilitates this evaluation. Successful results show that the proposed sequence matches the high resolution and accurate contrast of the reference sequence, despite the lower contrast-to-noise ratio of the respiratory bins. Radiologically, distinct anatomical structures are preserved in both sequences. However, the sequence is susceptible to motion blurring in areas of high gradient, such as the diaphragm. Despite this limitation, it offers a robust option for acquiring high-quality T2-weighted images in clinical practice, which are commonly used in radiotherapy treatments.

This research paper proposes a novel approach to developing safety-critical controllers for complex nonlinear control systems subject to input limitations. Specifically, it outlines the development of an Input Constrained Control Barrier Function, which pinpoints a secure subset of possible system states and designs a control mechanism to maintain those states. The devised controller can be optimized through an efficiently solvable quadratic program, enabling real-time application. Building upon earlier concepts of Higher Order Control Barrier Functions, ICCBFs demonstrate the ability to tackle a broader class of systems characterized by variable relative degrees. Finally, the paper showcases its efficacy through simulation examples in adaptive cruise control and spacecraft rendezvous.

In this work, domains are represented by equipping suitable families with an order based on set inclusion from specific mathematical structures. The focus here is on domain representations via approximation spaces with CF-structures, which involve introducing the concepts of CF-approximation spaces and CF-closed sets. It is demonstrated that the collection of CF-closed sets in a CF-approximation space, ordered by inclusion, forms a continuous domain and every continuous domain can be mapped isomorphically to the collection of CF-closed sets in a CF-approximation space. Building on this foundation, the notion of relations approximable by equivalence relations is developed using CF-closed sets in the product of two CF-approximation spaces, and the framework of CF-approximation space domains is extended to preorders in this context.

The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable exact algorithms forces practitioners to use time-consuming Monte Carlo approximations to achieve this goal. In contrast, we've developed an efficient method for calculating paired-permutation test results exactly. This exact algorithm takes significantly less time to compute than Monte Carlo methods. In particular, we observed a 10 times speedup when using our exact algorithm versus the commonly employed Monte Carlo approximation on a representative dataset of 20000 samples.

A comprehensive dataset of freight rates, shipping quantities, new ship prices, used ship prices, and scrapped ship prices has been assembled from 1966 to 2009 for the six primary shipping routes. Furthermore, instructions on combining and verifying datasets are provided using the knowledge of shipping industry specialists and former top executives. A descriptive analysis of previously unstudied market phenomena known as the "container crisis" is conducted with this data. Structural changes in the data variables are then identified to demonstrate how the dissolution of shipping monopolies affected market behavior.

We define loom spaces as a more general framework incorporating leaf spaces for pseudo-Anosov flows and link spaces for veering triangulations. Building on Gu\'eritaud's research, it is demonstrated that there is a veering triangulation inherently linked to every loom space, with this triangulation's realization being topologically equivalent to 3D space.

Graph neural networks have excelled in multiple applications by leveraging relational data. These models combine node features with the graph structure, creating flexible models that can adapt to specific tasks. However, their complexity, particularly with many network layers, can make them difficult to understand and explain. This limitation makes it challenging to leverage graph neural networks for applications where model interpretability is crucial. This research proposes a novel approach to simplify multi-layer graph neural networks by removing unnecessary network components, based on the importance of node features and graph edges. This method, tested on various datasets including Twitter trends, news co-aggregation, and Facebook page classification, demonstrates that the proposed sparsification can retain competitive accuracy while significantly reducing model complexity and enhancing interpretability by revealing the key factors that drive node labels from nodes and edges.

A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where subsequent vectors rely on feedback from previous inputs. Under such circumstances, the classic estimator can be compromised by a relatively low number of inferences, essentially making it vulnerable to manipulation. A more resilient estimator was proposed, which, albeit requiring quadratically more queries in proportion to the sketch size, significantly enhances the safety by a factor of k (with k being the number of key components) when compared to prior studies on CountSketch.

Building on previous findings, we observed in Part I that compact, singular areas within a manifold of positive scalar curvature can be conformally deformed to reveal related minimal geometries sharing key characteristics. This deformation preserves features like Ahlfors regularity, Poincare inequality validity, and tangent cones with positive scalar curvature. In Part II, we employ surgery-style arguments to successfully remove the singular sets present in these geometries.

A liquid consisting of superconducting vortices experiences an unusual response when subjected to a temperature and magnetic field that's perpendicular to those vortices. This Nernst effect can be extensively analyzed by considering a single plane and pair of quantities, specifically the viscosity at zero shear and the density of mobile entropy carried by the vortices. A key characteristic of this two-parameter system is that its response remains consistent with that of a perfectly conducting material in certain limits. This vorticular liquid's behavior also provides valuable insights into the underlying dynamics of superconductors, as it helps to reveal a relationship between their respective properties.

Effective management of controllable loads relies on the strategic deployment of aggregators that can efficiently convey their flexible capabilities, also known as flexible power, to system operators. This paper introduces a novel approach, the Real-Time Aggregate Flexibility (R-TAX) method, which is capable of forecasting the aggregate flexibility of multiple aggregators in real-time using machine learning. The R-TAX method is built upon the premise that the behavior of controllable loads can be modeled as random processes, and machine learning tools are utilized to predict how this behavior will unfold in response to various operational scenarios. The R-TAX method is then enhanced to ensure it adheres to key principles, including the guarantee that flexibility values remain within their established bounds and that the method remains consistent across different scenarios. The efficacy of the R-TAX method is demonstrated through the use of a case study involving electric vehicle aggregators, and the resulting predictions of flexibility are incorporated into model predictive control applications to ensure optimal system performance.

The recent interest in the stock market has made it crucial to develop effective investment strategies, as well as to accurately forecast stock prices.  The rise of Deep Learning has made it possible to create highly performant models for analyzing patterns and forecasting trends in the stock market.  Researchers have successfully combined Generative Adversarial Networks and Natural Language Processing to create robust models for stock price prediction.  A two-stage approach was proposed, where a BERT-based translator is used to generate a time series from text data, which is then fed into a Long Short-Term Memory network for price prediction.  A novel application of this method is showcased by using it to predict stock prices for Reliance Industries Limited on the Mumbai Stock Exchange.  The results of the study are visually displayed through various performance metrics, including mean squared error, mean absolute percentage error, and directional accuracy.  The source code for the study is available on GitHub.

One of the most intriguing phenomena in astrophysics is the common envelope (CE) phase of binary star evolution, where two stars are enveloped in the ejecta from one of them. This phenomenon is linked to several celestial objects such as mergers of neutron stars and black holes, as well as type Ia supernovae. During the CE phase, researchers have developed various models to describe its dynamics, but a unifying understanding is lacking. This study aims to present a unified approach to scattering binaries by introducing a potential function that encompasses different CE mechanisms like driven winds, aerodynamic drag, and the emission of gravitational waves. This model allows for a comprehensive visualization of how binaries evolve by producing a path function in parameter space. Our results indicate that a binary system will always evolve towards a tighter configuration, and the outcome of the CE phase is likely to be a merging of the two stars, although under specific conditions a stable configuration may be achieved. This could result in the formation of exotic objects such as magnetic stars, rapidly spinning supersoft X-ray sources, or low-mass black holes.

This research analyzes the potential of future electron-positron colliders, specifically ILC, CLIC, and FCC-ee, to study double Higgs boson production through a effective field theory (EFT) approach that describes interactions between Standard Model particles and the Higgs boson. By excluding triple-Higgs interactions and focusing on new physics beyond the Standard Model, the study investigates the sensitivity of various $e^+e^-$ colliders at center-of-mass energies of 250 GeV, 350 GeV, 365 GeV, and up to 3500 GeV, to the effective Higgs couplings. To better understand the S-channel process, the study conducts a theoretical analysis of the Higgs contact interaction and introduces an amplitude method for computing the virtual photon mediated scattering, resulting in closed formulas for the cross-section, which are verified against Monte Carlo simulations, providing accurate predictions for the differential cross-section, especially for the 3500 GeV collider.

We perform a covariant expansion of the Einstein-Hilbert action in powers of
$1/c^2$, achieving a non-relativistic gravitational field theory.
Our findings indicate that, in this limiting process, the action converges to
$\sum_n \left( W_{n+1}/c^n \right) $, where $W_1$ represents the Einstein-Uhlmann
term, $W_2$ the Einstein-Gross-Neveu term, and $W_3$ the Einstein-Hilbert term.
Furthermore, we prove that discarding $W_1$ and higher-order terms ($n\geq 2$)
yields a consistent non-relativistic gravity described by the Einstein-Hilbert
action, thereby establishing the validity of the covariant approach to
post-Newtonian expansions and revealing previously unidentified variations
of the gravitational field.

A new computational framework is introduced to speed up the calculation of localized shocks in a five-dimensional space that is modeled after a specific type of gravitational theory. By simplifying the complex equations governing these shocks, researchers can more efficiently solve them. A key step in this framework involves reorganizing them into a form that isolates the most significant components of the equations. This allows for a faster and more accurate simulation of the shocks' behavior, including during the difficult phase where they interact and scatter. When converted back to their original form, these simulations reveal the shocks developing thin layers and highly concentrated regions, as well as strong interactions and effects during the scattering process.

We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical solid moving through a layer of granular material, specifically polysterene and hydrogel grains, at various speeds and depths. The cylinder was oriented both perpendicular and parallel to its long axis as it moved, and we found that the drag it experienced differed significantly in the two orientations, a phenomenon we call anisotropy. This anisotropy varied greatly with the speed at which the cylinder was moved, its length compared to its width, and whether the grains it was moving through had high friction or little friction. Notably, the anisotropy increased more quickly in beds with low friction. Additionally, the drag experienced by the cylinder was found to be influenced more by its long axis than its ends. This phenomenon could be understood by studying the flow of sediment around the cylinder and estimating the drag experienced by its sides and flat ends.

Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation-driven gas outflows are linked to other properties of the galaxy. Our data show a nearly linear relationship between gas outflows and the product of the galaxy's mass and star formation rate. On average, about 10% of the gas being used to create new stars is being ejected into space. A key finding from our research is that in galaxies with higher rotation speeds relative to their diameter, the outflows retain more energy per unit of gas, and thus, the same star formation rate can produce different outflows depending on the galaxy's rotational curve. Our results support the concept of gas regulation as a crucial mechanism for maintaining the balance in the galaxy's population of stars.

A structured Bayesian optimization approach to system configurations is presented, called BoGraph, which combines elements of graph models and Bayesian optimization. We develop BoGraph to efficiently find optimal configurations in systems with numerous parameters and expensive performance evaluations. Traditional Bayesian optimization methods struggle with scenarios involving interactions among parameters, as they typically assume pairwise relationships and exclude tri-clausal relationships. BoGraph proposes a graph-based probabilistic model that encodes performance dependencies among parameters, which can be derived from performance data or expert knowledge. This model is then used to inform a structured Bayesian optimization algorithm. We test BoGraph on two computationally intensive systems: the NTLM authentication configuration and the DNA Sanger Sequencing workflow, and demonstrate its effectiveness through comparative performance with other methods.

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles.

Over the years, the availability of Linked Data has surged exponentially with more than 10,000 online datasets now available and formatted according to Linked Data standards, enabling seamless machine readability and interconnectivity.  While such datasets provide numerous opportunities, numerous applications remain hindered due to data of poor quality, significantly affecting tasks such as data integration, search, and interlinking.  Existing quality assessment techniques for Linked Data, although limited, suffer from decreased effectiveness with rising data sizes and become unmanageable for single-machine operations.  To address these challenges, our proposed DistQualityAssessment is an open-source, cluster-based implementation designed for comprehensive quality evaluation of large-scale RDF datasets, leveraging the processing capabilities of Apache Spark to distribute quality metrics computation and ensure scalability.  By doing so, we are able to accurately measure the reliability of Linked Data datasets and efficiently support data cleaning and integration, even with substantial datasets.

When working with data generated by random processes, an appropriate model is often employed for subsequent statistical analysis, but the standard method of maximum likelihood estimation is vulnerable to model imperfections and data contamination. As alternative methods, robust estimation techniques based on quantiles or data depth have been proposed, yet their effectiveness for continuous data has been limited, prompting the proposal of a novel method combining a penalty for data depth and establishing comparison criteria for robust estimation. The performance of this estimation procedure is found to be virtually indistinguishable from maximum likelihood estimation under ideal conditions and significantly superior in conditions of contamination, as demonstrated for processes observed at discrete time intervals, with the approach applied to estimate parameters for a Cox process and compared favorably to other robust methods, with results also presented for data from an exponential model and a Weibull model.

This study presents temperature maps for electrons within one Seyfert-1 galaxy and two Seyfert-1.5 galaxies, which are heavily active galactic nuclei. The findings show that the ionized emission from these objects often occurs at temperatures between 10,000 Kelvin and 30,000 Kelvin. What's interesting is that the temperature of the plasma seems to vary based on its location relative to the active galactic nucleus's absorption axis. Emission at 10^4 Kelvin is usually aligned with the axis, while broader areas exhibit higher temperatures. The data also show an apparent correlation between the temperature of the plasma and the intensity of the active galactic nucleus. However, the exact mechanism causing this phenomenon remains unclear. The temperature map for NGC 4945 is unusually complex, displaying both cooler and warmer emission patterns, including an area of very high temperatures just outside the galaxy's central dense disk. These findings are crucial in understanding how chemical emission works and can provide valuable insights for creating chemical models.

As IoT systems shift towards Edge computing and less reliable infrastructure closer to users, the complex environments of IoT networks require testing approaches that can handle both spatial and temporal variations. To achieve this, we developed a method for creating time-dependent, location-based test scenarios for IoT applications. Our framework allows for the design of multi-dimensional, real-world test cases that can be executed within the IoT system and on simulated platforms. We demonstrated our event-driven testing process by creating an automated tool and applying it to an indoor plant monitoring system.

The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has achieved precise measurements in two areas, namely neutral B meson mixing and CP violation, as well as in rare electroweak processes occurring in suppressed B-meson decays. This study concentrates on recent findings from the ATLAS collaboration, encompassing evaluations of rare occurrences like $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$ decays and the determination of CP-violating processes in $B^0_s \to J/\psi\phi$.

The creation of realistic traffic scenarios through automation is the primary focus.
Currently used approaches insert virtual characters into the environment using predefined rules but struggle to capture the intricate nature of actual traffic conditions.
These attempts have been limited in applying to various complex situations such as the existence of real obstacles, variations in lighting and seasonal changes, as well as traffic scenes involving public transportation and cyclists.
To address these shortcomings, we present an industry-based traffic scene generation method which utilizes a data-driven model to automatically insert a diverse range of elements, including buildings, road features, signs, vehicles, cyclists, and pedestrians into the environment.
Our algorithm is based on traffic scene elements that are obtained from an industrial database, requiring minimal adjustments to various parameters to create realistic environments.
Through this method, we are capable of generating building-grade detailed realistic traffic scenes that maintain a high level of coherence.
To further evaluate our algorithm, we conducted an online survey with 150 participants comparing our approach to manually inserting characters into the environment.
The survey results show our traffic scene generation method ranks higher than the industry standard, it also it is flexible enough to be applied to various complex situations such as public transportation, cyclists, and pedestrians.
On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model and find novel periodic measures that are linked to index-2 normal subgroups within its group representation.

A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited to preserving only one property and often lack high accuracy. This paper proposes a novel framework to address this challenge by proposing a framework to apply and analyze preconditioned Krylov subspace methods to both the exponential and logarithmic approximations. This framework is particularly useful given the maturity of preservation-based methods' implementations, enabling the proposed methods to be applied broadly to various equations and discretizations. Specifically, the methods are shown to achieve both a desired accuracy and the preservation of both a concavity property and an infinite norm bound. Additionally, the methods are shown to achieve both a desired accuracy and the preservation of an contractivity property, when using a structure-preserving discretization of the 2D Navier-Stokes equations.

A group of integer sequences can be classified as jointly ergodic if for every ergodic system with a measure-preserving nature, their average values, determined by iteratively applying the sequences, converge on average to a specific, integrated product that aligns with the original values. We have derived flexible criteria that can not only verify ergodicity across most known sequence combinations, but also enable resolution for some outstanding issues. Notably, our reasoning employs a novel ergodic variant of a technique initially explored by Peluse and Prendiville in establishing quantitative versions of the finitary Szemer\'edi theorem's application.

We developed three-dimensional hydrodynamic models to simulate the evolution of high-explosion-velocity supernovae within low-metallicity molecular clouds. The occurrence of grain formation was determined based on the presence of dust-grain-nucleating elements. We found that silicon dust forms readily around $0.01\ Z_\odot$ or higher, while carbon dust forms even at lower abundances. Because of the extremely high velocities generated by these explosions, dust grains are quickly shredded and dispersed into the surrounding cloud material. As a consequence, even minimal metallicities can facilitate the creation of both silicon and carbon dust. Although this process is inefficient, it paves the way for future stars and planets with the capacity to produce these elements.

Detecting three-dimensional objects at great distances is still a significant challenge in the three-dimensional object recognition domain. In fact, the performance of current methods significantly degrades when it comes to identifying objects in far fields. In fact, most evaluation protocols for three-dimensional object detection focus on near-field scenarios and exclude any objects located beyond certain thresholds, typically above no more than fifty meters. There is, however, a critical gap in object detection technology needed for applications in areas such as three-dimensional geographic information systems and geospatial mapping. To address this challenge, we propose a novel evaluation protocol for three-dimensional object detection in far-field scenarios. Our protocol assesses the detection performance of current models by dividing far-field and near-field objects into separate categories. Our experimental evaluation shows that current state-of-the-art three-dimensional object detectors struggle to accurately detect far-field objects. Interestingly, our analysis indicates that radar data offers a significant advantage over camera data in detecting far-field objects. Moreover, we observe that training detectors exclusively on far-field objects leads to a noticeable improvement in their performance in such scenarios. Lastly, we introduce a novel end-to-end far-field three-dimensional detector, which outperforms existing two-stage detectors when using radar data.

Chemical reactions can be comprehensively understood through a key metric, namely, the potential energy surface (PES). However, a closely related concept, the ground state surface (GSS), can also serve as a substantial indicator of molecular and chemical behavior. The GSS provides essential information about the stability of molecules, the feasibility of chemical reactions, and various other aspects. Despite its significance, calculating the GSS of complex systems poses substantial challenges. In this investigation, a quantum machine learning approach is investigated for generating the GSS of systems. Initially, a set of compact quantum support data is obtained, and a quantum support vector regression model is used to construct a representation of the GSS. The model's training and inference can be efficiently carried out using the PQSVMTR source code, and it is demonstrated that even for systems with over 50 electrons, the QSVR model can accurately predict the ground state energies of electron configurations that have not been explicitly evaluated.

Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on non-rigid registration. For laparoscopic liver surgery, we integrate an organ model derived from preoperative CT scans with a thin-shell surface model obtained intraoperatively using laparoscopy. By leveraging relative landmark positions from the endoscopic image, we refine the biomechanical properties of the organ model, thus enhancing the correspondence between the simulation and the actual surface of the specimen. This approach yields an efficient coarse-to-fine registration method, producing a robust start point for optimizing the match between the simulated and the observed surface through surface-surface matching.

For a static, spherically symmetric spacetime, research has focused on conformal matter collineations within the energy-momentum tensor. The overall structure of these collineations is determined under non-degenerate conditions, with fifteen distinct, independent forms found. However, when the energy-momentum tensor becomes degenerate, the associated conformal collineations exhibit infinite degrees of freedom. Moreover, specific degenerate subcases may still harbor non-degenerate Ricci inheritance collineations.

A popular self-supervised scene flow estimation method involves training a neural network using a loss function based on the bi-lateral approximation of the optical flow.  This study proposes enhancing this process by introducing a metric learning loss during training.  Initially, we explore using the triplet loss, but find its impact on performance to be minimal.  Subsequently, we introduce a novel loss called the Adversarial Triplet loss, which aims to minimize the distance between an anchor and a randomly selected negative in the output flow field.  Conducting experiments on the KITTI Flow dataset reveal that our method yields remarkable results, outperforming the state-of-the-art method DCP by a significant margin.  However, when evaluated on the KITTI-2012 dataset, our method's performance exceeds the available ground truth by a considerable amount, indicating potential areas of improvement.

In recent years, AI networks, specifically those based on artificial neural systems, have significantly outperformed competitors in a wide range of tasks including image recognition, sound analysis, and language interpretation. However, widespread use of such models was previously hindered due to their massive computational requirements for initial training and real-time operation. Neuromorphic computing and spiking neural networks (SNNs) are now seen as a promising alternative, offering efficient on-line processing and reduced power consumption while keeping performance levels comparable to conventional models. To date, research on leveraging SNNs for effective and energy-savvy operation around the target device has mainly concentrated on optimizing the existing models' activation functions and classifiers. This presentation delves into an innovative approach using a spiking random forest to enhance both the accuracy and energy-efficiency of classification tasks around the target device, with the aim of surpassing current methods.

This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field at finite temperature, applying the MIT bag model. Furthermore, we derived the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter in the presence of a strong magnetic field, and subsequently, we examined the structure of spin-polarized strange quark stars across varying temperatures and magnetic fields.

A Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property in a graph implies that each perfect matching can be combined with another to create a Hamiltonian cycle. This concept was first introduced by Las Vergnas and Haggkvist in the 1970s. Our research aims to explore the relationship between cubic graphs and 3-edge-colourings to identify those whose every perfect matching corresponds to a colour of the graph's edge-colouring. This property is equivalent to stating that each edge is part of both a perfect matching and a Hamiltonian cycle, which in turn, is equivalent to stating that each edge can be combined with another to create a Hamiltonian cycle. A necessary condition for a graph to possess this Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property is that it must be 3-edge-colourable. In this research, we will define a subgraph, C*, of the circular connectivity-connectivity class of cubic graphs, and prove that any graph belonging to C* that is also 3-edge-colourable possesses the Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property, and therefore, so does any graph whose edges connect to a specific 2-connectivity class, and any hamiltonian graph of a specific hamiltonian connectivity class, CH*.

Recent research on block designs by Amarra, Devillers, and Praeger, involving specific quadratic polynomials, shows potential connections to two influential conjectures. The Bunyakovsky Conjecture would yield a crucial implication - infinitely many instances of the required designs. A vast number of prime values of the involved polynomials have been found and their quantities match closely the expectations based on a refined variant of the Bateman-Horn Conjecture. Although the infinite prime values of the polynomials have yet to be definitively confirmed, the results provide significant support for both the Bunyakovsky and Bateman-Horn Conjectures.

This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. In addition, Timeloops rectifies several shortcomings of existing system call filtering techniques, addressing issues like inefficiency, lack of adaptability, and manual customization. As a result, Timeloops offers a streamlined, transparent, and effective solution, successfully limiting unauthorized system calls in over 900+ tests across a wide range of programs and services.

Investigating global $B-L$ symmetry within the Standard Model is necessary due to the anomaly cancellation requirements which necessitate three right-handed neutrinos that enable the natural generation of small Standard Model neutrino masses through the seesaw mechanism. Within an extension of the Standard Model featuring a $B-L$ symmetry, we introduce a pseudo-Goldstone boson dark matter framework where the imaginary component of a complex $B-L$ Higgs field constitutes the dark matter present in the universe. The universe's dark matter abundance is dictated by the Standard Model Higgs boson-mediated process, yet its interaction with nucleons via the exchange of Higgs bosons is heavily suppressed due to its pseudo-Goldstone nature. As a result, the proposed model avoids constraints imposed by direct dark matter detection experiments. Furthermore, we pinpoint model parameter regions that replicate the observed dark matter density in accordance with the Large Hadron Collider data and the findings from the Inferno and EGE dark matter detection experiments.

This study develops a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter where target appearance probabilities are organized on a grid. A streamlined variation of the Rao-Blackwellized point mass filter predicts the density of unobserved targets, with their distribution approximated as Gaussian for initially located targets and a Poisson density for the rest. Contrary to conventional approaches, the poem-based component is not integrated out, as it is correlated with the part based on past observations. Instead, the distribution of the poem-based component is directly predicted using the measurement and noise models, provided the history of observations. A direct prediction formula is derived to maintain the consistency between the two components based on the covariance of unobsected targets. The proposal includes all necessary theory and can be adapted for general use. A new algorithm is introduced in the context of sensor management, where the system observes targets through a set of available sensors and reports their positions based on a particular density of unobserved targets. The algorithm demonstrates that optimal predictions of the two components are interconnected, with the poem-based component's prediction relying on the observation history and the part-based component's prediction depending on the distribution of unobserved targets.

This study examines the null controllability of a population model that includes an interior degenerate diffusion component. By first establishing a new Carleman estimate for the adjoint system in its entirety, and subsequently deriving a relevant observability inequality, we aim to demonstrate the existence of a localized control action capable of driving the population towards extinction within a finite time frame.

The dynamics of a soccer game, particularly near the end, can significantly influence the home team's chance of winning. A study examined this concept by dividing home matches based on the team's position on the field in the final minute before the 85th minute. The research demonstrated that the location of players can impact the home team's chance of victory. To explore this, a study developed a simplified soccer simulation and evaluated the house edge at different game states. The investigation highlighted the importance of positioning in influencing the home team's chance of winning. Furthermore, to potentially improve the home team's performance, the research applied deep reinforcement learning to learn the value of specific actions. The results showed that specific tactics, such as forming a 5-player wall in the corner of the field, could be beneficial.

High-resolution subsurface modeling for oil and gas exploration and geohazard prediction depends on advanced seismic imaging and interpretation.  One key approach, Extended Source Waveform Inversion, combines seismic data interpretation and subsurface modeling by utilizing the boundary between oil reservoirs as a virtual source of a secondary seismic event.  This concept of "virtual fracking" proposes inducing secondary seismic events at no cost to frack oil deposits to generate large-scale seismic events.  Although promising, this technology requires further optimization of its underlying processes before it can be safely and effectively deployed in the field.

We've developed an all-optical technique for producing optical nonreciprocity on a microchip, achieved through the process of quantum squeezing a specific mode in coupled resonator systems. A key factor in this method involves applying classical coherent light in a one-way fashion to parametrically pump a nonlinear resonator. This selective pumping generates a pair of sidebands with differing phases and amplitudes. As a result, when a probe beam interacts with the squeezed resonator, its experienced transmission is altered based on both the squeezing and the phase of one sideband. This phenomenon of nonreciprocity can be intensely amplified due to the process of superadditivity. Additionally, we've modeled the system's response and discovered that nonlinear effects can be utilized to control the nonreciprocal transmission, enabling strong asymmetry even with a weak linearly linearized transmission.

We have presented the results from the AstroSat analysis of the high-mass X-ray binary X-ray pulsar IGR J19294+1816 during its Type-I outburst in October 2019. Timing and spectral data from the 14.4 ks observation revealed the spin period to be 12.454 s, with significant spectral features. The average count rate during the observation was 557 cts/s, and the spectrum showed a hard component with a photon index of 1.49. A quasi-periodic oscillation with a period of 6.1 s was detected in the power spectrum with a quality factor of 9.6. The spectral fit also revealed a thermal component at a temperature of 0.44 keV and a narrow cyclotron line at 41.4 keV with a depth of 11.6 keV/cts/s. These findings provide insight into the physical processes occurring in the system during its active phase.

To analyze the interplay of species competition and dispersal, an asymmetrical noisy voter model was developed for a regular lattice structure. The model allows one species to colonize nearest-neighbor sites, while another species can settle at any distance but is less successful in doing so. The model includes external noise, which can lead to random species swaps in the lattice. The combination of these dynamics results in various species competition outcomes, including the exclusion of one species, distinct population coexistence, or bistable coexistence dependent on the initial species distribution. The model shows that an abrupt transition occurs as immigration intensity surpasses a critical point, causing the irreversible decline of the species with shorter dispersal range. The model was examined using theoretical calculations, a spin-model mapping approach, and Monte Carlo simulations.

Ancient sundials served as primary timekeepers before the invention of mechanical clocks, with the classical Islamic civilization utilizing the Sun's daily movement to determine prayer times, often relying on sundials for this purpose. This knowledge eventually spread to Indonesia through Islamic cultural influences. Indonesian sundials developed as a reflection of local advancements in astronomy, technology, art, and architecture, with historical examples warranting detailed documentation and study, though often overlooked in existing literature. To collect necessary spatial and temporal information on these sundials, a citizen science initiative could be implemented, addressing research inquiries while promoting science education among the general public. This concept has been proposed as a framework, referred to as the Suryakala-Nusantara program, to explore the scientific and pedagogical value of sundials in the Indonesian context.

This research focuses on an integrated data and energy transmission network, which incorporates D2D communication. This hybrid network allows a central hub to transfer data to those in need and supply power to those who require it. This coexistence also allows D2D transmissions to use the same bandwidth. This integrated network is assisted by a intelligent reflecting surface. A optimization problem is formulated to maximize the data transfer efficiency between the central hub and other devices by adjusting the surface intelligence, the transmission rates, and the power distribution. This problem is highly nonlinear due to the coupling of variables in the objective function. A solution is provided to this problem by first decoupling the surface intelligence optimization and then formulating a sub-optimal solution to determine the optimal surface configuration. This allows the rest of the transmission and power distribution to proceed. Numerical simulations demonstrate the feasibility of this approach and highlight its potential benefits.

The surge in telework needs has highlighted the potential benefits of fully
automating and controlling experiments remotely. This work presents the technical
advancements of creating a two-dimensional LDV measurement system using a single-
point LDV system via a remotely controllable and automated setup. The document's
aim is to expedite the development of similar setups for this kind of application,
which is highly versatile and can be applied to various scenarios including both
air-based acoustic signal-driven samples and mechanically induced samples.

The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is subject to debate 
given their varying suitability for particular applications. Our study delves into 
alternative designs of phase plates specifically tailored to mitigate spherical 
aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). Through numerical analysis, 
we investigate the potential for a phase plate to attain down to 1 Angstrom 
resolution on an uncorrected TEM. By examining various design parameters 
including pixel resolution and phase distribution, we identify the characteristics 
necessary for a phase plate to attain this level of performance. Interestingly, 
it is found that while a traditional phase plate is incapable of achieving this 
resolution, alternative designs can attain up to 0.95 Angstrom. These electron 
bright imaging phase plates, if controlled by a field-programmable gate array, can 
also function as spherical aberration correctors in modern TEMs, given that pixel 
aberrations can be circumvented with a sufficiently high pixel count.

The success of data-driven dialogue models heavily relies on their ability to accurately encode user input to generate relevant and effective responses. While it is common to evaluate the generated text for its semantic and syntactic quality, the underlying representation of this encoding is often overlooked, which can hinder the model's performance in anticipating the next utterance. This work argues that merely assessing text generation metrics from a encoding representation is insufficient, and proposes incorporating task-oriented evaluation to evaluate the efficiency of encoder representations in capturing context to effectively predict the subsequent dialogue turn. Furthermore, we propose Generative Dialogue Pre-training (GDP), a novel approach that leverages a task-oriented task to evaluate the efficiency of encoder representations in predicting the next speaker's response, and demonstrates the effectiveness of GDM in improving both generation and task-oriented performance compared to existing baselines and pretrained models.

DL-based LiDAR place recognition in autonomous vehicles relies on a robust feature descriptor to capture 3D surroundings and efficiently match them to map elements. Due to the vast data and complex 3D environment, extracting relevant features from point clouds is a challenging task. This paper presents an attention-based deep learning network that point clouds can be processed point-by-point, improving point extraction performance and reducing point clouds to two directions for faster and more accurate descriptor generation and matching. Furthermore, to adapt to varying point cloud point densities, this paper also proposes a novel point sampling method. Experimental results using the KITTI dataset demonstrate the proposed method's superiority over conventional methods.

Streaming high-quality video, whether it's in HD or ultra-high definition, demands transcoding to ensure optimal performance on cost-effective infrastructure. This study develops an mathematical model to predict the transcoding of video files on cloud platforms that utilize various types of computing devices. The model evaluates the use of these platforms for video transcoding tasks, taking into consideration the efficiency and cost of transcoding compared to purchasing new HD or ultra-high definition videos. By doing so, the model can assist companies in making informed procurement decisions based on their needs and budget.

We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic density-density correlation of massless Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which is applicable at finite temperatures. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material.

Continuous speech leads to consistent prosody patterns, yet current speech synthesis models often disregard context. These systems fall short when it comes to producing high-quality paragraphs, necessitating a system that integrates contextual elements. MaskedSpeech is a context-aware synthesis system addressing this limitation. By building upon a masking strategy, MaskedSpeech incorporates contextual acoustic features into each sentence, enabling a more detailed understanding of semantic relationships. Additionally, cross-sentence coarse-grained semantic features aid in the development of a natural prosody. Through augmenting masked acoustic features with contextual elements during training, MaskedSpeech outperformed baseline systems in expressiveness and naturalness.

We provide explicit definitions for the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves in a model that includes a Klein-Gordon equation and an anharmonic oscillator. We also conduct a comprehensive analysis of the linearized equation's spectrum at the solitary wave state.

Q-ball studies in a single symmetry theory are common, yet the field can be more expansive, allowing for the examination of theories featuring multiple symmetries in a more general context. In this paper, we explore this broader scenario, analyzing both the standard and advanced limits within this theoretical framework and identifying essential conditions for existence in the more complex scenarios. Additionally, we identify a previously unexamined Q-ball state, which we term 'cored', and demonstrate that it could possess stability under specific conditions; a more detailed investigation into cored Q-balls is also presented.

We investigated a cyclic universe containing holographic dark energy with different infrared cutoffs, excluding the Big Rip singularity. The study reveals that, in the absence of interaction between the cosmos sectors, the HDE model using the Hubble radius cutoff behaves like a cosmological constant within cyclic cosmology. Furthermore, we discovered that cyclic patterns of contraction and expansion may occur for both interacting and non-interacting universes, provided that the Granda-Oliveros cutoff is selected for the HDE's energy density.
