Under these conditions, an EDM constraint of 9*10^-36 e cm could be achieved with FHC, leveraging semi-invisible final states and displaced vertices to benefit from the enhanced precision.

We investigate decoding of rank metric codes under the assumption of a symmetric error matrix. Our analysis yields two main conclusions. Firstly, we show that for code rates less than half, there is a diverse class of rank metric codes capable of accurately decoding any symmetric error, even those of maximal rank. Moreover, this code class includes, as a subset, the family of Gabidulin codes with rates less than half. Secondly, we propose a method for correcting symmetric errors of up to n-k rank, which can be applied for code rates greater than half. Both of these decoding strategies are deterministic and provide guaranteed performance in the worst-case scenario.

Building upon previous work by \cite{Ferrara:1971vh}, \cite{Ferrara:1973vz}, we develop a comprehensive integral representation of conformal block operators in CFT$_2$, specifically for spinning primary fields. Notably, this integral expression can be interpreted as a product of two weight-one conformal primary field operators. Leveraging the AdS/CFT correspondence, where the CFT$_2$ theory is dual to three-dimensional anti-de Sitter space, we express the AdS$_3$ conformal block operators in terms of two scalar fields residing in the AdS$_3$ space.

Future experiments to study the Cosmic Microwave Background will be able to measure a crucial parameter, n_t, with high precision, however this measurement requires reducing the noise from lensing of the foreground power spectrum. To effectively reduce this noise, we need to develop an efficient method for reconstructing the gravitational lensing effect on the sky, this can be achieved by finding a way to map the original sky back to the pre-lensed state. The performance of lens reconstruction is limited by the number of independent pieces of information that can be extracted from the observed data. Upcoming experiments such as the Cosmic Microwave Background Stage-4 will provide significantly more information, thus enabling the use of more complex models to improve reconstruction efficiency. The current methods for lens reconstruction based on traditional approaches are no longer sufficient for these experiments, we have developed a new approach by utilizing machine learning, in this case a neural network, to improve the efficiency of the process. In this study we evaluated our method under various scenarios including a scenario where primordial tensor perturbations are present in the data and we found that our method can extract almost as much information from the data as theoretically possible and it results in unbiased results with an efficient use of the available data. Furthermore we demonstrated that this method is also effective when using incomplete data and it results in lens reconstruction with an noise level that is several times lower than the standard quadratic method.

In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson established a local and combinatorial approach to calculating Pontrjagin classes for differentiable manifolds. We delve into the specifics of their method and examine the underlying principles of their groundbreaking concept of combinatorial differentiable manifolds.

We obtained 15 optical photometric observations and four spectroscopic observations of SN 2020jfo, a Type II-S supernova, between 14 days and 244 days after it peaked. Based on available data, we obtained host galaxy and SN magnitudes. Using these, we calculated the SN's light curve, which showed features consistent with other Type II supernovnas, notably an extended "plateau" period. From the photometric and spectroscopic data, we derived an explosion energy of $1.08 \times 10^{51}$ erg, a mass of $0.21 M_{\odot}$ for $^{56}$Ni, and a pre-explosion mass of $6.5 M_{\odot}$.

To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a concept called multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics. This configuration involves dividing an LE mirror into multiple sections and using each one to direct X-rays onto a single shared image sensor. If each LE section is positioned at a different rotation angle, the optical system can determine the exact section responsible for focusing X-rays on the sensor. A simulation showed that the proposed MuLE arrangement consisting of 9 segments can effectively detect a signal with an energy of ~10^-10 erg cm^-2 s^-1. Furthermore, this system is highly effective in determining the source direction of an X-ray transient, which is critical for its use in future wide-field X-ray transient monitoring missions on small satellites.

We establish a level set formulation for partial uniform ellipticity with symmetric concave functions, implying a viable strategy for studying second-order fully nonlinear elliptic and parabolic equations.

To investigate the structure of dark matter, a deep learning framework was implemented and used to explore the impact of velocity and density information on the formation of halos through $N$-body cosmological simulations. A Convolutional Neural Network was trained on an initial snapshot of a dark matter simulation, with the goal of predicting halo masses at a given point in time. Results showed that including velocity information significantly improved prediction accuracy by a factor of 10 when the simulation represented typical cosmic conditions. Furthermore, the model identified the critical threshold of mass concentration required for the formation of dark matter halos. A similar investigation was conducted on a simulation with exaggerated initial conditions based on the $\Lambda$CDM model, and a notable discrepancy between the dark matter simulation and the $\Lambda$CDM simulation was identified in terms of mass concentration at the virial overdensity, a finding that may have important implications for the interpretation of mass function data in dark matter simulations.

Converting an audio recording of music into a symbolic format is a challenging Music Information Retrieval task, specifically piano transcription. This study proposes a semi-supervised technique using low-rank matrix factorization methods, notably Convolutive Nonnegative Matrix Factorization. Utilizing a single audio recording of each individual note, we demonstrate on the MAPS dataset that our proposed semi-supervised CNMF method surpasses conventional low-rank factorization techniques, but slightly lags behind leading deep learning approaches while facing broader applicability issues.

We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying assumptions about angular velocity, in favor of specifying angular velocity directly as a function of fluid element trajectory and time. This direct angular velocity parameterization avoids assumptions prevalent in the Eulerian approach, which may not hold under varying conditions. Furthermore, our method eschews mapping techniques, in effect solving Einstein's equations in a non-physical coordinate system. This approach has significant theoretical advantages over the Eulerian method. We successfully demonstrated its practical application by simulating the evolution of a rotating star with the duration of its day as a key variable.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is obtaining a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. In order to reduce this burden, we present a novel strategy that models can utilize to learn document structures implicitly from raw images. This approach, which we call "unlabeled fine-tuning," allows for the adaptation of pre-trained CRF-based models to specific document types using unlabelled images. By leveraging the document structure that these models capture, we can present a simplified data format that focuses on the textual content only. This format, which we call "structurally-labeled data," can be easily utilized to create high-quality training datasets for CRF-based models.

The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, analyzing waveforms produced from neutron star-black hole mergers is impeded by the unknown parameters of the neutron star's tidal deformability. Traditional methods for extracting physical parameters from these complex waveforms are computationally costly and call for novel, robust methods that can generalize well to this diverse range of signals. In response, we present a deep learning approach utilizing a sequence-to-sequence autoencoder network, which we trained and evaluated across a comprehensive dataset of neutron star-black hole merger waveforms. This model outperforms previous methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency, enabling the reliable estimation of physical parameters from these signals within a factor of 10 in computational time. Furthermore, it excels in generalizing to events with low black hole masses when provided with appropriate training data.

The adverse effects of social determinants of health on the quality of care should be addressed by healthcare organizations and researchers. Identifying individuals who are vulnerable due to social factors can be achieved through the classification of demographic information from existing data, which often includes key information such as race, gender, and gender identity. In this research, we explored the capability of deep learning models to infer social determinants of health from demographic data that primarily consists of demographic information. Our initial data analysis indicated that social determinants of health are not explicitly captured in demographic data. Consequently, we developed a multi-task learning framework that utilizes demographic data to detect social determinants of health, indicated analysis findings by demonstrating that deep learning models have an informative influence toward this end, and evaluated various neural network approaches including linear, multi-layer, attention, and transformation-free methods. Our key discovery indicated that demographic data contains implicit information about social determinants of health, which can be leveraged to enable deep learning models to detect these factors.

This study is centered on a two-part swimmer known as the scallop, which transitions through varying dynamics across two different fluid environments. We resolve two optimal control scenarios, one focused on achieving the fastest time to relocate the swimmer and another on finding the most energy-efficient method using periodic control to move it between predetermined positions. Leveraging the simplicity provided by limiting switching to one point and taking advantage of the underlying structure, we can obtain a complete description of the solution's behavior. For a specific instance where the swimmer's body shape influences the situation, we also identify optimal strategies involving multiple switching points.

Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million anonymized users in four major US cities, spanning pre-pandemic to post-pandemic periods. It reveals a significant drop (by 15% to 30%) in urban diversity during the pandemic, with protective measures having the most pronounced negative impact. Analysis of individual behavior shows that increased caution in adopting protective measures led to decreased diversity as people stuck to familiar neighborhoods for safety. Notably, those who continued engaging in social activities without regard for diversity contributed the most to maintaining diverse urban interactions. Understanding cautions in this context is crucial for promoting diverse urban settings that are conducive to economic and social growth.

Three-dimensional simulations of high-mass young stellar objects reveal that their surrounding disks break apart into multiple gravitationally significant objects, such as disk fragments and mergers of jet-wind structures, by the time t = 400 days. These objects may contribute to the growth of the central star through accretion, although the amount of mass that actually crosses the innermost disk boundary is about half of their total mass due to interactions with the jet-wind structure and the magnetic field. Alternatively, angular momentum can be transferred to the central star through the magnetic field, causing a magnetic rotor effect and rapid accretion of the disk objects. This phenomenon could be the cause of the episodic accretion theory, which posits that massive stars grow via distinct phases and speeds. Furthermore, some of these disk objects, particularly black holes, could be the source of observed variations in the spectra of massive stars and their associated bipolar lobes.

Buchholz established a practical approach to understanding massless two-dimensional scattering theories. Within this approach, we've demonstrated that a given theory is completely characterized by its asymptotic algebra and scattering matrix under specific conditions. By applying a procedure grounded in von Neumann algebras, we've derived multiple families of interacting wedge-local nets, one of which is closely related to Buchholz-Lechner-Summers' chiral CFT deformation. We've also successfully isolated the strictly local elements in another instance. Furthermore, using endomorphisms on the U(1)-current net and the free fermion net developed by Longo-Witten, we've constructed a large family of wedge-local nets.

Implementing 5G antennas across a region is crucial for delivering 5G connectivity. Yet, little attention has been given to assessing 5G cellular tower exposure among children and occupants of sensitive locations, including schools and medical facilities. To address this gap, this research evaluates 5G cellular tower exposure among children, students, and facilities in sensitive locations. We outline a method to determine 5G cellular tower exposure, then apply it to calculate the average 5G cellular tower exposure experienced by children on various paths, students inside classrooms, and occupants of hospitals and medical centers. Notably, calculated 5G cellular tower exposure values are found to be significantly lower than South Africa's safety guidelines for 5G frequencies.

This research investigates how a uniform shear flow influences the behavior of water waves in an infinite, two-dimensional domain, specifically those with nonzero constant vorticity. We sought to analyze how a uniform shear flow affects weakly nonlinear, surface gravity waves through the use of Hamiltonian formulation and Hamiltonian transformation techniques. By applying these methods, we obtained a new approximate model describing the interaction of waves and shear flow, then utilized direct integration to solve this model and obtain an exact expression for its Hamiltonian. Furthermore, we performed numerical simulations to understand the behavior of the model and found that its dynamics are significantly impacted by the vorticity of the flow, with both qualitative and quantitative differences observed in both the presence and absence of the shear flow. Our study contributes to the field of physics by extending the understanding of the interaction of waves and shear flow, a topic that has received considerable attention over recent years.

In this proof, a modified Stokes formula for differential forms is demonstrated on a specific class of locally convex spaces. To establish this result, the surface layer theorem is utilized as a key tool. Additionally, an expression for the operator adjoint to the exterior differential is obtained for differential forms within a specific class relative to a measure defined through differentiation. This connection was previously demonstrated with assumptions more restrictive than those employed here.

Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing environments is a significant challenge for mobile robots. Mobile sonar ranges, which are commonly used in robot navigation, are affected by noise that can significantly impair performance. In applications like hospital or warehouse navigation, this noise is especially problematic. In this study, a noisy-2D sonar fusion method has been proposed to enhance layer-based navigation in dynamic 2D environments. The proposed method projects the sonar sensors onto a high-resolution virtual grid, allowing for precise obstacle detection and obstacle-avoidance in complex environments. To validate the method, simulations were conducted using a 2D dynamic environment and a mobile sonar robot, which demonstrated the method's ability to navigate safely and efficiently, even when encountering moving objects.

The prevalence of false news is not a new issue but one that has been with us for as long as there have been legitimate and deceptive stories. The rapid advancement of social media has significantly accelerated the spread of fake news at no cost. This research explores the potential of using summarization techniques to detect false news, by generating concise versions of articles and analyzing them in combination with original content. We investigate a range of summarization models, comparing their generated outputs to manually written summaries, before incorporating these summaries into a larger framework to distinguish between real and false news. Our findings suggest that the use of automatic summaries can enhance fake news detection, outperforming a conventional binary classification approach.

This research investigates complex systems that follow stochastic patterns by using mathematical structures known as random field models. The study focuses on analyzing a specific aspect of these systems – the geometry of their parametric space – using statistical tools to simulate and model the systems' dynamics. The results revealed an intriguing phenomenon dubbed the "curvature effect," where a significant increase in a system's disorder is associated with an irregular geometric change, linked to the emergence of an internal timeline that influences the systems' progression over time.

This research targets resolving secrecy concerns for nonorthogonal multiple access users by introducing an alternative decoding order method. First, we mathematically quantify the total possible decoding order options. We then propose an effective decoding order approach that guarantees positive secrecy rates for each user and, through computation, determine the feasible secure decoding order quantities. To minimize complexity in determining the best secure decoding order, we also present an efficient yet suboptimal solution strategy. Notably, the proposed suboptimal solution achieves around 137% improvement in performance over a relevant benchmark solution.

When applying dimensionality reduction techniques to datasets with anomalies, L1-PCA has been a well-liked alternative to conventional PCA due to its robustness in recent years. This study focuses on an under-explored version of rotationally invariant L1-PCA and develops an iterative optimization approach using proximal alternating linearized minimization and a form of extrapolation tailored to its two-block representation. Moreover, the algorithm is theoretically proven to converge linearly to a stable point, and this result is also guaranteed for the restricted case of variance explanation maximization with binary data, and numerically demonstrated through simulations.

Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing models possess linguistic knowledge that can, in turn, be leveraged to guide the annotation process. In this work, we employ BERT, a neural language model, to facilitate the semantic labeling of a game-based interaction dataset called EMO20Q. Following a pilot study, we determine that BERT can effectively identify question emotions with greater accuracy than the original annotators, or at least match their performance. Consequently, BERT can serve as a reliable tool for correcting inaccurate annotations.

Kopczyński and Waśkiewski enhanced the concept of energy over infinite graphs by extending it to grouped terms. They observed that determining whether a verifier can indefinitely increase a game's score of edge word products is equivalent to supplying a strategy with this capacity, and found connections to parity games when the group is abelian and generates-free. Their work also established a connection between the longest-finite product problem and parity games when the group is Z^2. This paper builds on their findings by investigating this topic over totally ordered groups, proving that the energy problem is resolvable for groups isomorphic to Z, Z^2, and Zn, but not for any Hr and for any totally ordered group larger than any Hr.

The subclass of magnetic Cataclysmic Variables, asynchronous polars, still lacks a comprehensive understanding. Asynchronous polars are a category of polars characterized by their white dwarf spin period differing significantly, whether longer or shorter, from their binary orbital period. The detection rate of asynchronous polars in soft gamma-ray observations is disproportionate, implying that they might naturally have more intense X-ray spectra. In order to explore the link between a Cataclysmic Variable's synchronization status and its X-ray emission pattern, we conducted a comparison between standard and asynchronous polars using their entire sample set, discovering a possible association between harder spectra and the former, albeit without conclusive statistical evidence.

This project's primary goal is to investigate the integration of the Reduced Basis Method (RBM) for Fluid-Structure Interaction (FSI) problems, considering both a monolithic and a partitioned approach. A secondary goal is to compare these two methods and evaluate how they meet specific criteria. A reference solution will be used to assess the results, as will a reduced order model based on the Galerkin method and a directly discretized structure. Two distinct reduced basis strategies will be examined: the first involves solving the fluid and structure problems separately, whereas the second employs a fully coupled approach during reduction.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, these systems can struggle in large-scale environments due to their sensitivity to initial conditions and distortions caused by local changes in the map. To address this challenge, our research focuses on developing a hierarchical topological map representation for navigation in unknown environments. This allows the robot to utilize a minimal graph for navigation, while also accommodating multiple disconnected subgraphs when returning to previously visited areas. Our approach employs clustering algorithms to build a graph-based map from place supervisory training data and enables the robot to collect data and construct new subgraphs as it explores new areas. We validate our approach through simulation and with real robots, and demonstrate its versatility with several navigation scenarios.

The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 SemEval OffensEval Task is the subject of this paper. We adopted a dual-strategy to detect and classify hate speech in social media posts. For subtask A, a BERT-based classifier was adapted and achieved a high macro F1 score of 0.8286 in evaluating test data, thereby ranking 3rd among 103 competitors. Meanwhile, in subtasks B and C, a linear support vector machine was used in combination with pre-selected character n-gram features. Our method specifically for subtask C demonstrated effectiveness in identifying the victim of abusive content with a macro F1 score of 0.5343, and ranked 27th out of 65 participants.

One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that affects atomic motion within the interferometer, making it possible to measure this effect through atomic interference patterns. Based on the $10^{-12}$ g accuracy achieved in atomic gravity measurements, it's theoretically possible to measure expelled local magnetic field strengths at levels as precise as $10^{-14}$ Tesla.

We investigate the emergence of magnetocaloric effect (MCE) in two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides due to their proximity with a ferromagnetic substrate, specifically a MoTe$_2$ monolayer on EuO with a heat source. Using a tight-binding model that accounts for proximity-induced exchange and Rashba fields and temperature via Fermi statistics, we simulate this system and reveal substantial changes in spin-polarized entropy and specific heat induced by temperature variations. Our study indicates that the heat source can effectively heat the isolated MoTe$_2$ region, and that the MCE in this system is dominated by the Rashba field at the Fermi level. Moreover, we observe the presence of valley-polarized MCE in this system.

We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model. We demonstrate that a quantum hydrodynamics model which incorporates both phenomena yields accurate results, particularly as the gap narrows, in contrast to a local response model which generates unappealing results such as divergent fields and excessive energy losses.

The Calculus of Constructions, introduced in 1985 by Coquand, has been a driving force in the development of dependently typed programming and higher-order constructive logic over the past 25 years. This influential theory has influenced research in programming languages and type theory, contributing to the creation of languages such as Coq and Agda through its numerous extensions. This survey presents an in-depth analysis of the various proofs demonstrating the strong normalization property of the Calculus of Constructions, emphasizing both the underlying similarities between these proofs and the unique goals of the researchers involved.

We invite undergraduate students and early graduate students to an educational introduction to one-dimensional topological phases, focusing on the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. This will include discussions on entanglement using the correlator method and von Neumann density matrix, as well as geometric phase, polarization, and transport characteristics, all with consideration of electron-electron interactions. Hands-on numerical experiments guided by publicly available codes are used to convey the value of using topological toy models for student learning.

In the case of a finite admixture model whose components and weights are unknown, techniques from stochastic convex geometry help us determine how the number of identifiable components changes in response to an increase in the amount of collected data. Additionally, placing a Dirichlet process prior on densities within a defined range enables us to recover a measure that narrows to the specific identifiable components, thereby providing a connection with Choquet's Theorem.

We derived a two-loop amplitude formula for four graviton supermultiplets in AdS$_5$ times S$^5$ using a preamplitude construction, confirming the findings of Huang and Yuan. The amplitude is built from a set of invariant variables, and we demonstrated that this method accurately reproduces known six-point tree-level and two-loop vacuum minimality conditions, as well as satisfying the finite part of the two-loop Bethe-Ansatz equations. The construction is then employed to investigate four-point interactions and vacuum stability for various short BPS operators, including B$^2$, D, W$^4$, and non-BPS operators up to four fields, with most analyses conducted up to two-loop order. The preamplitude is shown to satisfy the conditions for four types of operator states, with particularly promising two-loop vacuum stability observed in the B$^2$ operator state. The document also outlines possible extensions of the AdS-CFT correspondence to incorporate two-loop effects.

High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified DynaSOAr, a high-level parallel programming framework built on top of CoArray, a GPU-compatible object-oriented programming framework.  DynaSOAr extends DynaAr, a parallel memory allocator for arrays of structures, by providing a hybrid data model that includes both individual structure variables and pointers to memory-filled structure fields.  This new framework features a C-style parallel object syntax that can be easily integrated into C++ code using a macro-based approach.  As a result, developers can create highly optimized, parallel applications with excellent performance and portability across multiple programming languages and platforms.

This paper investigates the boundedness of a diverse set of operators, including those generated by the Calderón-Zygmund operators and the fractional integral operator, on generalized mixed Morrey spaces. Additionally, the article examines the boundedness of the commutators of these operators on the same space. Furthermore, specific applications are considered to obtain the boundedness of several operators, such as the Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator and the Calderón-Zygmund singular integral operators, on generalized mixed Morrey spaces.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of the isolated Mn adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while localized spin polarization on Nb atoms showed marginal influence. Additionally, by scaling the exchange field of the Mn adatom, the transition from normal to superconducting state Nb was observed, exhibiting state-specific sensitivity to the exchange field. By examining a dimer oriented perpendicular to the crystallographic direction of the Nb atom, a magnetic exchange interaction between the Mn atoms was seen. The exchange field in the dimer system exists on the Mn atom near the Nb and results in a modified YSR splitting. This work demonstrates that first principles based on the spin-orbit coupling can accurately describe YSR state properties, providing a reliable theoretical tool for the design of magnetic atoms, nanostructures, and their placement on the surface of a superconductor to manipulate YSR states.

Our proposal, FourierMask, integrates the Fourier series with implicit neural networks to create instance segmentation masks. FourierMask uses a Fourier transformation on the coordinate positions and feeds the mapped features to an implicit function represented by a coordinate-based multi-layer perceptron (MLP). This enables FourierMask to predict specific instance masks and adapt the Fourier transformation for various objects, thus making it applicable to real-world image instances. Since implicit functions operate seamlessly over the input domain, FourierMask can generate higher-resolution masks with fewer input pixel coordinates. By integrating a renderer and a loss function, we evaluate FourierMask's performance on the MS COCO dataset using both standard and high-resolution metrics. Experimental results show that FourierMask consistently outperforms other implicit instance segmentation masks and surprisingly competes effectively with prominent explicit segmentation masks.

This study examines how the discrete nature of the frequency spectrum for a non-compact manifold embedded in a higher-dimensional space affects its boundary points, focusing particularly on the Hausdorff dimension of those boundary points. Specifically, if a flat, extrinsically bounded two-dimensional surface is mapped onto a bounded, three-dimensional convex area, and the boundary points have a certain measure, the frequency spectrum will be discrete only if those boundary points form a countable set. This study also proves a related theorem and explores its implications.

Current retrievals of cloud optical thickness and particle size using passive satellite imaging techniques fail for complex convective clouds. These failures stem from the limitation of using one-dimensional radiative transfer theory to analyze three-dimensional cloud morphologies. Cloud tomography offers a promising alternative to treating clouds as fully three-dimensional objects. Developing efficient forward solvers for three-dimensional radiative transfer will be crucial for applying this method from space. By acknowledging the existence of optically thick cloud cores, where scattered photons do not contribute useful information, we can refine future 3D retrievals. Investigating this phenomenon using data from the MISR and MODIS satellite imagers, we identified key insights to streamline cloud tomographic reconstruction. Notably, we determined the veiled core of optically thick clouds to typically be at radii of 200-500 m, a radiance threshold of 0.5 times the cloud's optical depth is recommended, and tomographic reconstruction with total photon data is found to be nearly as accurate as using only scattered photons.

We examined how a laser pulse with a changing frequency impacts its passage through a sub-wavelength target and the acceleration of ions. Our investigation focused on a laser pulse with frequency rising over time and observed a significant improvement in ion acceleration compared to a counter-intuitive result when using a frequency decreasing pulse. Our investigation into the self-induced transparency phenomenon revealed that a chirped laser pulse generates a more dense plasma channel, thereby facilitating the acceleration of ions to higher energies.

The space telescope TESS has discovered a planetary system named TOI-712, which contains at least four planets and is centered around a K-dwarf star. This system is considered unique because it is one of the few TOI candidates that resides in a relatively bright and nearby area, located 241 parsecs away, where the host planet in the habitable zone has an effective temperature similar to our Sun. Using various observation methods, researchers have obtained consistent measurements of the system, which includes relative planet masses obtained through radial velocity measurements. TOI-712 is a rare example of a young planetary system, which is in the adolescent stage of development. Mass estimates for two transiting mini-Neptune planets, which are located inside the habitable zone, have been estimated to be 4.35 times the mass of Earth and 6.57 times the mass of Earth. If these planets have comparable bulk compositions to our Solar System's mini-Neptunes of a similar size, their equilibrium temperatures would be significantly lower than expected. Furthermore, TOI-712's planets are migrating inward due to their interaction with the stellar disk of gas and dust, which is relatively cool.

We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2, using the PBE0 hybrid DFT method. Subsequent analysis involved comparing carbon and nitrogen doped TiO2 with PN co-doped TiO2, focusing on how this combination affects the material's overall characteristics. Our findings highlight that carbon acts as an n-type dopant, creating both donor and acceptor levels within the TiO2 band gap. In contrast, nitrogen introduces only a shift in the O 2p valence band, maintaining TiO2's overall behavior. Notably, nitrogen located at carbon sites transforms it into an isoelectronic defect, resulting in a net n-type characteristic in the rutile TiO2 material. Carbon and nitrogen also exhibit spontaneous spins, with the carbon atom displaying a net spin of 2.

This letter describes the inspiration and an analytical method for detecting the production of top-quark pairs in the Large Hadron Collider through the identification of protons emitted at the front end. I demonstrate the feasibility of identifying the semi-elastic process, where one top-quark decays into a $W$ boson and a $b$-quark and the other top-quark is damaged. I also find that specific cuts on momentum and transverse momentum can enhance the sensitivity to new physics interactions by a factor of $4.6$ over standard searches. The results suggest that identifying the production of top-quarks in a elastic collision is difficult to achieve at the LHC.

Observations of the intra-cluster medium with X-rays allow for a detailed examination of its turbulent structure, which is significant as it contributes to the structure functions of scalar quantities, measurable via X-ray imaging and spectral analysis. However, the resolution of such measurements is limited by the properties of X-ray detectors and clusters' mass, leading to statistical and systematic uncertainties that affect the determination of flux, density, and temperature maps. This study builds on previous research and aims to quantify the impact of these measurement uncertainties on the estimated second and third order structure functions, using simulations of thermalized plasma with the added influence of turbulent fluctuations. The authors find that the estimated values of these structure functions from the images can significantly deviate from the true values in the plasma simulations, with the discrepancy increasing as the spatial resolution decreases. Furthermore, the impact of these measurement uncertainties is more pronounced for temperature than for flux or density, and for third-order structure functions, it is difficult to distinguish the influence of turbulence from that of the uncertainties. These estimates may be corrected by applying scaling factors derived from the properties of the X-ray mission being used, as demonstrated to work for SPT-SZ and Planck measurements.

In 1993, Erdos and Galvin pioneered upper density problems within Ramsey theory, specifically the problem of identifying the highest $\lambda$ value such that in every two-edge coloring of the complete infinite graph, there exists an infinitely large, monochromatically colored subgraph resembling $F$ with an upper density of at least $\lambda$. We expand upon this research by providing a lower bound for this $\lambda$ value, with specific cases where the lower bound is equal to existing upper bounds for structures like cliques and odd cycles, and a $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}$ value for triangles that surpasses the former record of 3/5.

Located at the heart of the Milky Way lies the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), a distinct ring-like formation, where analysis of the 870 $\mu$m continuum map from ATLASGAL, obtained via the APEX Telescope Large Area Survey of the Galaxy, revealed notable anisotropic anisotropy in gas density within this region. Utilizing a modified scalar anisotropy metric developed by Glazebrook and Broadhurst, researchers discovered a significant 11$\sigma$ indication of 2D elliptical structure in the CMZ at a position angle of 75$^\circ$. This aligns with the long axis of the CMZ ring and the major axis of the Galactic bar. A secondary, circularly shaped 4$^\sigma$ feature was also identified, oriented perpendicular to the primary anisotropic pattern. This secondary feature may correspond to spiral patterns or a superposition of bar and bulge components as seen in near-infrared observations. This research is part of a larger study aimed at exploring the 3D spatial characteristics of dense gas cores within the CMZ on a global scale.

This paper introduces a groundbreaking method to identify Bell's Palsy solely by analyzing a person's eye movements in a video. We have observed that patients with Bell's Palsy encounter difficulty blinking their affected eye, creating a noticeable disparity in blinking patterns between the two eyes. Building on existing research, our work exclusively focuses on eye movements rather than entire facial images. This unique approach ensures individuals' anonymity and facilitates the interpretability of AI-driven conclusions. We have devised a novel metric called Blink Symmetry Index, quantifying the symmetry of blinking patterns and serving as a crucial feature in our eye-focused detection system.

Our analysis highlights the benefits of using qudits instead of qubits in scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d, specifically regarding their tolerance to errors. When measuring the mass gap and scattering phases of sQED, our findings indicate that simulations utilizing qutrits of depth-one are substantially more reliable than their qubit-based counterparts. For both observables, the reliability gap between qutrit and qubit simulations is at least ten times greater, which suggests that qudits offer significant improvements in reducing errors.

Research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced through interactions between intense lasers and solid materials, specifically within the context of strong-field quantum electrodynamics. However, the polarization properties of these positrons are not controllable via current methods. Our study proposes the use of sub-wavelength thinnest solid densities to achieve polarization control of the generated positrons. By simulating the interaction between the intense laser and these materials, we found that the resulting positrons exhibit high levels of spin polarization, with values of 0.1 to 10 times 10^-1. The polarization is strongly influenced by the polarization of the used laser materials and can be controlled to over 50% through a process known as spin precession. The conditions for this research are within reach of existing or soon-to-be-available laser and target systems, with the potential to produce up to 10^11 positrons per laser pulse, which will be available as fully polarized electrons once captured in storage rings.

Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to their highest order, making up a substantial fraction of the group's total size. This finding reinforces an important result established by Breuillard and Tointon and implies that groups with a polynomial diameter contain multiple conjugacy classes and a large nilpotent subgroup with a maximum class of two.

This research develops a fully integrated CMOS temperature sensor that is capable of wide voltage operation and precise temperature measurement in three distinct ranges. The proposed sensor uses a sub-threshold biasing technique to create three unique voltage-dependent current differences in three separate sub-threshold transistors, in addition to using a biasing circuit based on BTBT. A binary search-based ADC is used for efficient and low-power temperature conversion, making the sensor's performance adaptable to the expected operating range, thus improving resolution and reducing power consumption. The sensor's inaccuracy is corrected using process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) calibration, with the biasing circuit contributing to precise measurement and the ADC contributing to the sensor's resolution and low-power consumption. The 80TSMC 0.18μm process-processed sensor underwent 1250h long-term testing and 12 process chips' characterization, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed design. The sensor's low-power consumption, high resolution, and precise measurement are demonstrated in the experimental results, including the use of the sensor in a mobile app and a portable device for real-world applications. The inaccuracy of the three temperature ranges is 1.4°C, 2.8°C, and 5.6°C, with corresponding resolutions of 240m°C, 120m°C, and 60m°C, demonstrated as 1.4°C, 2.8°C, and 5.

Long-standing hypotheses propose that advanced stellar types, including A-type, may develop instabilities due to magnetic activity akin to that seen in the Sun.  Although the Sun's magnetic fields are confined to low percentages of its total mass and remain largely uncomputed in most models, the situation changes for subgiants and giants whose expanded volumes can contain their magnetic fields within the core region, contributing up to one-half of their total mass.  This potential for magnetic fields to significantly influence the internal dynamics of evolved stars has been a topic of intense research, with numerous studies demonstrating the potential for field-induced stellar oscillations or even overall stability loss.  In a related development, a class of magnetic fields that are symmetric around the stellar axis and remain unmixed with the surrounding plasma has been found to exist within the interior of these evolved stars. This discovery prompted further investigation into the possibility of such fields sustaining themselves within these celestial bodies. Our study builds upon previous work by computing the velocity components of a fluid moving around a stationary, axisymmetric magnetic field in the interior of a star with constant density.  By applying a linear stability analysis to this system, we discovered that, with certain constraints on the magnetic field configuration, both axisymmetric and non-axisymmetric perturbations decay over time.  Our results indicate that magnetic fields of this type can exist as stable configurations within these evolved stars.  Notably, fields with this property could potentially persist for billions of years, with important implications for their detectability via observations of

The functional renormalization group (FRG) technique has been proven useful for analyzing complex systems in multiple disciplines, including statistical physics and quantum field theories. Researchers solve FRG problems by establishing a set of flow equations that reflect the adjustments made to a system as a parameter of coarse-graining changes. In this paper, we introduce an innovative strategy to address flow equations that draws on parallels between these equations and conservation principles found in fluid dynamics. We then demonstrate the feasibility of adapting sophisticated numerical methods from fluid dynamics to tackle the complexities arising from the renormalization group, specifically the appearance of non-analytic behavior. Additionally, our findings facilitate fresh perspectives on renormalization group flows, including an exploration of how the nature of the flow might be altered by regularizing the frame through the choice of regularization function. Finally, our approach is validated using one-dimensional and multi-dimensional models that follow the same principles, including the $O(N)$ model.

Music enthusiasts still heavily depend on conventional search engines like Google for pop music, which is surprising considering how indispensable the internet has become in everyday life. Our innovative proposal is for a music-centric search engine called Pied Piper, which will serve as a comprehensive meta-search tool, enabling users to find relevant music information by searching for lyrics, song metadata, audio, or a blend of any of these options.

This PhD research focuses on exploring specific geometric constructs over Lie groupoids and differential stacks. Building on the foundations laid out in [arXiv:1609.01521, arXiv:1609.01524, arXiv:1609.01527, arXiv:1609.01530], the study involves a series of related topics. It begins by establishing the correspondence between connections and 2-connections on principal groupoids, followed an in-depth investigation of the Atiyah algebroid and its associated representations. The study also involves exploring the links between Riemannian and non-commutative differential geometry. Additionally, there is a direct connection between leafwise differential geometry and the geometry of the holonomy groupoid of a foliation. Finally, the study involves the development of the theory of connections with a fixed curvature on a principal bundle.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows and those that are not.  The former exhibit characteristics consistent with a lower mass threshold of approximately 0.03 solar units, whereas the latter indicate a higher mass threshold of around 0.13 solar units.  The 850 $\mu$m spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of the cores generally display thermal characteristics aligned with a warm dust population.  The outflow-associated cores are found to be more numerous above 3 solar units in comparison to the non-outflow-associated cores.  The analysis of SEDs and the extrapolation of the 1.3 mm SEDs to the sub-millimeter and far-infrared wavelengths, assuming a graybody model with a 30 K temperature, does not exhibit statistically significant differences between the two groups.  The difference in the masses likely arises from a combination of factors, such as the effect of outflows on the 1.3 mm mass estimation and the influence of temperature variations, as well as the dynamic state of the gas within the cores, which could result in the non-outflow-associated cores containing higher masses but spread across a broader spatial area.

Godel modal logics can be regarded as an extension of intutionistic modal logics with prelinearity. This study explores algebraic and relational semantics for Godel modal logics built upon the duality between finite Godel algebras and finite forests, a type of poset. The research considers subvarieties of basic Godel algebras with two modal operators, alongside their respective classes of forest frames, both with single and double accessibility relations. These relational structures serve as prelinear counterparts to traditional intuitionistic modal logic semantics. The study specifically examines two expansions of finite Godel algebras: the addition of Dunn axioms, common in positive classical and intutionistic logic, and the addition of Fischer Servi axioms. The research provides Jonsson-Tarski-like representation theorems for different types of finite Godel modal algebras with operators.

LiDAR point clouds offer valuable measurements for complex environmental settings, allowing for updates to digital elevation models and applications such as glacial monitoring and landslide detection. However, interpreting LiDAR data can be a time-consuming and labor-intensive process, especially when it comes to identifying features such as trees or buildings. Our research presents an open dataset and a comprehensive benchmark for various tree and building detection methods based on LiDAR data. We evaluated multiple tree and building extraction algorithms and found our approach to be more efficient than conventional methods, allowing for real-time assessment of forest parameters and building locations. Notably, our research results indicate that our proposed approach is more accurate than state-of-the-art methods, with lower errors in mean absolute percentage and correlation coefficients.

Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods to the Gegenbauer polynomials, enabling the derivation of adjacent relations that maintain positive definiteness, and ultimately, the construction of an infinite family of polynomial sequences on the sphere.

The source of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) has remained a major puzzle in high-energy astrophysics for many years. To shed light on this enigma, researchers are correlating UHECRs with high-energy neutrinos as they offer a direct and magnetically unbiased glimpse into hadronic interactions of cosmic rays. This paper introduces three new strategies to link neutrino and UHECR arrival directions, aiming to uncover any potential spatial correlations that could reveal the nature of UHECR origins. These methods include a machine learning-driven search for 3-system UHECR-UHECR-UHECR associations, refining the UHECR-high energy neutrino match, and employing all-vs-all analyses to maximize any potential spatial overlap. The results of these analyses are then compared to both theoretical predictions and a previous UHECR-UHECR match match. Based on our findings, the current data do not provide sufficient evidence of spatial correlations, though future experiments with more comprehensive datasets may offer more insights in the coming decades.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip, and stasis. The accuracy of the previously proposed law of inertia-Weber number transition for Toblerons is also demonstrated for these foam structures.

This report details our methods and outcomes in developing a deep learning
network for classifying skin cancer, utilizing 101 different sample classes
available at the website http://isikdergisi.com.tr/ResmiSayfa/1345. The dataset
is characterized by an uneven distribution of samples, which poses a challenge
for the accuracy of the cancer detection task. To address this issue, we
proposed modifying the outlier samples within the dataset to create a more
balanced dataset, thereby improving the performance of the classification
models. We designed a novel network called CE-LAN (Convolutional Entropy-Attention Network), which leverages entropy-weighted attention modules to automatically
adjust the weight of each sample, and by using the adjusted attention as a
classification confidence score, which can be utilized to only selectively
modify the dataset to create a more balanced dataset, thereby improving the
performance of the cancer detection task. Moreover, the CE-LAN network focuses
on extracting more discriminative features from the images, and through hard
sample mining, it automatically identifies the most challenging samples for
classification, and then employs a contrastive loss to force the network to
extract more descriptive features for network training. As a result, we present
an effective solution to handle the uneven distribution of data in classification
problems, and achieved state-of-the-art performance, with 99.96% accuracy in
distinguishing between melanoma and non-m

The steady-state behavior of an elastic membrane, situated between two fluids of differing densities in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell, subject to external pressure, is examined in a study that also compares its inextensibility to that of an extremely elastic membrane. When the inner fluid density surpasses the outer fluid density, the membrane exhibits a Rayleigh-Taylor-like instability caused by centrifugal force, competing with the curvature and tension-driven restorative forces, thus dictating the size of the developed finger. Numerical computation techniques are utilized to analyze not just nonlinear finger patterns but also modes with both circumferentially confined folds and branches that occur with variations in the rate of rotation and imposed pressure. Bifurcation diagrams representing a variety of states, including both reflection-symmetric states and asymmetric states, are presented as functions of the Lagrangian pressure, whereas in non-rotating cells, only states that exhibit reflection symmetry can exist in the presence of two branches.

Building on a novel theory, microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics, we've successfully applied it to examine the irreversible process of free expansion in a two-chamber system. Despite a noticeable change in the phase space volume, we thermodynamically calculate the work and heat for this process using the proposed method. To our surprise, the heat obtained equals zero, which seems to contradict Boltzmann's principle. To clarify, we've used a simple model to examine the process step by step and found that thermodynamic calculations hold for each individual microstate. Consequently, we've concluded that the thermodynamic first law can be successfully applied to systems undergoing free expansion, even when the system's boundary changes, as long as we consider trajectory-based calculations.

Scientists have identified the presence of two specific isomers, 1- and 2-ethynyl-1,3-cyclopentadiene, of ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C$_2$H$_2$C$_4$H$_4$) originating from the TMC-1 molecular cloud. Using a sub-millimeter telescope, a distinct spectral pattern was matched to this molecule's rotation-vibration transition. After analyzing data from multiple observational sessions, researchers concluded that both ethynyl cyclopentadiene isomers are present and have an aggregate abundance relative to HC$_3$N of $1.4^{+1.4}_{-0.7}\times10^{-4}$. The abundance ratios of various cyclopolyyne molecules place TMC-1's chemical composition among the richest known in this category in the interstellar medium. The C$_4$H$_4$ cycle's fraction is notably lower than the C$_2$H$_2$ acetylene cycle's, a finding that supports a model in which a reaction with C$_2$H which has a positive activation energy barrier controls the accetylene cycle but is restricted by a barrier to the cyclopolyyne cycle. Consequently, the relative scarcity of cyclopolyyne cycles can be anticipated in the interstellar medium. The observed ethynyl cyclopentadiene abundances correspond to a cyanogen/carbon monoxide

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel mechanism known as look-ahead attention, which assigns significance to target words that have been generated, rather than just adjacent ones. When integrated with conventional attention, this mechanism yields significant performance boosts with no need for extra model parameters. Notably, the best result achieved uses no look-ahead attention to skip three source tokens and yields a 0.3 improvement in BLEU score compared to baseline models.

The significant discrepancy between growing data storage costs and declining hard drive prices led to the development of the Grid. From a translational perspective, the Grid's creation was a response to the challenge of managing and managing costs associated with growing data. The grid's creation was shaped by a translational approach that considered both supply and demand factors, as well as the socio-technical environment, resulting in the development of grid computing. A key element of the grid's design was the introduction of a flat pricing model that valued computing power by energy consumption, ultimately giving rise to the dominance of data centers in the industry.

A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous characteristics. This model has been applied to a flat, Friedmann-Robertson-Walker universe, and we have derived a compact form for the Hubble parameter in this context. Our analysis reveals that the model's parameters are directly related to those of the visible universe. A detailed examination of the model's evolution phases and its alignment with observational data was conducted through the study of the deceleration parameter, energy conditions, and the statefinder system, ultimately revealing that the dark fluid's behavior is equivalent to that of a dark energy-like universe in its final stages of evolution.

In educational settings, curiosity is a vital cognitive trait that fuels a
learner's desire to acquire new knowledge and engage in active learning.
However, due to its abstract and intangible nature, accurately assessing
curiosity remains a significant challenge. Furthermore, traditional
measurement techniques often fail to capture the real-time fluctuations in
students' levels of curiosity. To address this limitation, our study introduces
a novel, non-intrusive method for measuring both individual and group
curiosity by analyzing the eye movements of learners working together on
curiosity-driven tasks. Our approach combines data from eye-tracking devices
and curricula to create a dynamic profile of how individual and group
curiosity change over time. Utilizing this method, we were able to investigate
how curiosity fluctuates in real-time as small groups of learners interact,
and we discovered that curiosity levels can vary significantly, both
individually and collectively. Our findings also suggest that curiosity can
be a powerful catalyst for curiosity, as learners' interest in a subject can
be amplified when they are exposed to the perspectives of peers. To demonstrate
the effectiveness of our approach, we applied our method to an inquiry-based
learning task, where we observed that our eye-tracking based measures of
curiosity correlated well with more established techniques for assessing
students' levels of engagement. Overall, our study suggests that our eye-
tracking based method provides a reliable and valid tool for accurately
assessing the complex and ever-changing

Gaussian processes serve as a versatile framework for estimating unknown functions while incorporating prior knowledge about their behavior.  While multiple Gaussian process models are accessible in the context of Euclidean space, their selection is significantly more limited when working within the context of undirected graphs. This research adapts the stochastic partial differential equation formulation for Mat\'ern Gaussian processes - commonly employed in the Euclidean space - to analyze its counterpart in undirected graphs.  By demonstrating that the maturing Mat\'ern Gaussian processes on graphs can be effectively represented using a hybrid form, this study enables the application of efficient optimization techniques, such as the algorithm proposed in Rasmussen & Williams (2006), while ensuring that the learned models adhere to pre-specified constraints, such as those found in and around the given graph.

The effective management of urban roads requires real-time monitoring of travel times within the network. A large network of sensors, however, is both costly to operate and energy-intensive. The rise of urban ridesourcing fleets presents an alternative solution, as these vehicles can be utilized to reduce the number of dedicated sensors required and lower the associated costs of monitoring. Through the development of a compressed sensing algorithm for road networks, we demonstrate that the presence of ridesourcing cars significantly improves the performance of time-based sensor configurations, ultimately allowing for the creation of a more efficient, accurate, and cost-effective urban traffic monitoring system.

This study investigates the implications of the J/psi decay into visible gamma rays and invisible particles for field theories describing neutrinos, dark matter, and their potential interconnections. By analyzing a hypothetical process, constraints are placed on the parameters of neutrino and dark matter, including their majoron interactions and mass ranges. Furthermore, simulations were run using CT10 parton distribution functions to predict J/psi production in neutral current scattering at the LHC, taking into account neutrino interaction-induced J/psi production.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We then establish order conditions for these new methods of order p with q=p stage order and demonstrate them through specific examples up to order four, further confirming their efficiency in solving non-stiff problems via numerical experiments and theoretical convergence analysis.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series (MFTS) and real-world applications, including the analysis of intraday temperature curves and remote sensing images of vegetation. Additionally, MFSSA is made available through the Rfssa R package for user convenience.

Deep learning-based automated essay scoring systems are increasingly employed by educational institutions and testing agencies to evaluate numerous applicants and students. Unfortunately, these evaluation models are susceptible to manipulation through both known and previously unknown attacks targeting both classification accuracy and regressive score predictions. Research into the vulnerabilities of deep learning models in education has been limited, likely due to the absence of comprehensive automated essay scoring datasets. To address this gap, this research examines a real-world AES system in detail and demonstrates its susceptibility to both established and novel attacks. Although these attack strategies are attack-specific and not directly comparable, they all reveal the attackability of the AES system in question. The primary limitation of our attack methodology is its reliance on access to the target AES model, which cannot be applied to ranking or selection tasks. To counter these attacks, three potential defenses are proposed.

The power law decay $p(t,x) \sim t^{-\phi(x,\sigma)}$ is a universal phenomenon, $t$ being time, $p(t,x)$ a quantity with an enduring persistence, and $e^{-\phi(x,\sigma)} \in [0,1]$, the ratio of persistent particles, dependent on precise parameters $x$ and $\sigma$. The ratio's value is determined by the distribution of $x$ and $\sigma$ with values above their respective thresholds. The exponent $\phi(x,\sigma)$ can be universally defined, $x$ and $\sigma$ influencing it.
