The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. Until now, it was unclear if this plasma source could achieve helicon mode, which is essential for it to function effectively. A study was conducted to verify this capability, and it was found that plasma density and potential distribution match theoretical predictions of helicon discharge. Additional features of this discharge, such as a boundary layer of plasma, were also observed. It was further confirmed that this plasma source can operate in the helicon mode over a wide range of plasma potential, and can produce plasma densities necessary for experiment.

In comparison to conventional chemical pesticides, microbial pesticides exhibit numerous advantages, which can be modelled through a system where entomopathogenic nematodes are used to eliminate and concurrently suppress the population of target insects. This system aims to manage pests through a continuous nematode release mechanism, where the model's equilibrium and Hopf bifurcation periodic solutions are analyzed for optimal pest control, which is further confirmed by numerical simulations and case studies.

A challenge in pathology image analysis is nucleus segmentation, which is made more difficult by a lack of precise annotations and numerous overlapping nuclei. To reduce this problem, researchers focus on nucleus detection, although some methods struggle with analyzing large histopathology images, resulting in many false positives and missed detections. To tackle these issues, most studies process small patches and combine the results, but this research diverges by handling whole images and producing more accurate results. The proposed framework, a novel single-shot network called W-Net, uses an efficient convolutional architecture to produce accurate nucleus detection and segmentation results, outperforming previous methods in both tasks.

Let's consider a non-Archimedean local field of characteristic not two and denote it by F. Additionally, let G be either a specific type of special orthogonal group with an odd number of dimensions or a symplectic group with a specific dimensionality, denoted as SO(2r+1)(F) or Sp(2r)(F) respectively. This paper focuses on establishing the local converse theorem for the representation of G. To this end, for two given irreducible admissible generic representations of G, with shared central character and gamma factors, our result stipulates that these representations are isomorphic. To prove this, we draw from the Cogdell, Shahidi, and Tsai framework of partial Bessel functions and the categorization of irreducible generic representations. Furthermore, our result extends the earlier works by Jiang and Soudry as well as Q. Zhang, by expanding on their results for the cases with supercuspidal representations in a wider set of characteristic settings.

Xiong and Liu previously provided a definition for graphs G that have hamiltonian n-th iterated line graphs, L^n(G), where n is 2 or greater. In this study, we examine whether an L^n(G) graph possesses a hamiltonian path, and offer a definition for G to achieve this condition. Additionally, we apply this definition to set multiple upper limits for a graph's hamiltonian path index.

Cell death due to pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can contribute to the high cytokine levels seen in severe cases of COVID-19.  Pyroptosis is primarily initiated through the NLRP3 inflammasome's activation, primarily by SARS-CoV-2 viral components that trigger pattern recognition receptors.  Studies have shown that some viruses can stimulate various immune receptors, allowing for the design of targeted therapies to prevent pyroptosis and the resulting inflammation.  In this study, we created a single-cell mathematical model of pyroptosis to examine the complex, stepwise process of viral pattern recognition receptor activation, NLRP3 inflammasome assembly, gasdermin D cleavage, and the resulting pyroptotic cell death.  Our model gasdermin D dynamics showed a good fit to experimental data, illustrating the cell death's two phases.  We applied the model to various cases of viral pattern recognition receptor activation levels and found intermediate cases produced the cell death dynamics similar to experimental observations, whereas fully activated or uninactivated receptor cases did not.  We also tested the model with interventions that could block viral pattern recognition receptor activation or the inflammatory signal processing of the assembled inflammasome, and found both could prevent pyroptotic cell death, making them potential pyroptosis-inhibiting strategies.  The cell death model's outputs may help inform the development of anti-inflammatory drugs that can prevent the pyroptosis-driven inflammation linked to severe

External influences affecting states and reward signals can hinder reinforcement learning by introducing unanticipated fluctuations in the reward signal. This concept is mathematically formalized, and the conditions are identified under which an environment involving uncontrollable state variables can be broken down into two separate components: an environment solely affected by the uncontrollable state and reward variables, and an environment defined by the variables that can be controlled. Additionally, a condition for reducing the complexity of these variables in Monte Carlo policy evaluation is established, leading to potential acceleration of this process. This acceleration could be applied across a broader range of reinforcement learning algorithms. Two methods are devised for identifying the uncontrollable state variables, and the results from applying these methods to multiple test environments show a notable increase in efficiency and a potential for speeding up the reinforcement learning process.

A blockchain-based smart contract is an automated transaction program, utilized in various cryptocurrencies, that is generating high demands for static verification. To fulfill this need, our project HELMHOLTZ is introduced, capable of checking the correctness of Refinement-Type Java to Tezos Michelson, ensuring transaction safety and contractual compliance of smart contracts. As a part of this, HELMHOLTZ incorporates types into the target language, enabling Michelson contracts to be annotated with a refinement-type version of Refinement-Type Java, and the specifications defined in these annotations to be checked by SMT solvers.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process.

In a three-dimensional spacetime, Einstein's gravity theory is replaced by Chern-Simons gauge theory, redefining mass and angular momentum as conserved currents. A new, action-based description is found for a specific type of black hole, characterized by hair made of a scalar field, where the hair's profile is set by constant Chern-Simons gauge fields. A general class of these black holes is described analytically. Further, by exploiting the symmetry of the model, the hair profile can be made to decay rapidly, transforming the black hole into a smooth, horizonless object.

Theories of supersymmetric Yang-Mills with algebra so(4N) can have non-invertible symmetries, which can be represented by branes that are invariant under a dual D3 and carry a fraction 1/4 of the total algebra. Through the analysis of the behavior of these branes under a process of dualization, we can determine their unique properties and the way they transform.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, the measurement of lateral displacement remains relatively crude due to limited sampling in the ultrasound beam direction. This research introduces a technique called Virtual Source Synthetic Aperture (VSSA), which increases lateral displacement resolution and accuracy. VSSA involves calculating the propagation of the synthetic aperture in a virtual reversed source, also known as Virtual Reverse Propagation Synthetic Aperture (VRPSA). VRPSA demonstrates a higher sensitivity to mechanical properties variation than its conventional synthetic aperture counterpart (PSA), resulting in more accurate displacement maps. When compared to PSA, VSSA exhibits reduced error in voxel-based analysis for both linear and logarithmic transducers, with the improvement becoming more pronounced at higher frequencies.

Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning.

The concept of linear extensions is a well-studied one within the field of order theory, but an unexplored area is that of linear colorings. In this work, we investigate $r$-colored Boolean lattices $[k]^{[k]}$ to determine the minimal $k$ for which your given $r$-closed poset $\mathcal{P}$ contains a poset isomorphic to $\mathcal{P}$ in each of the $r$ colors. For chains, this problem was previously addressed by Glebov, Grinberg, and Tardif, who established an $O(\log^{265}\ k)$ bound. In this study, we focus on $V$-shaped chains and tree-width $t$ and prove that several related parameters are $O(\log^{2}\ k)$, $O(\log^{6}\ k)$, $O(\log^{6}\ k)$, and $O(\log^{2}\ k)$, respectively. Notably, we resolve an open question posed by Glebov, Grinberg, and Tardif by showing a $O(\log^{6}\ k)$ bound for chain-width $t$.

In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$.

We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We then connect the two levels by deriving a stochastic transition function that accounts for the outcomes of the individual games' strategies. This two-level framework can be applied recursively to complex environments, creating a detailed narrative that evades capture even in the face of a highly powerful, non-stochastic pursuer.

Inspired by classic counterintuitive phenomena, a particular n-tuple $(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ within the range [0,1] is classified as 'cyclic' when there exist unique, independent random variables $(U_1, \dots, U_n)$ where the probability of $U_{i+1}$ being greater than $U_i$ matches $x_i$ for $i$ from 1 to n-1, and $U_1$ being greater than $U_n$ matches $x_n$. A 'nontransitive' n-tuple is defined similarly, but with $x_i$ representing the probability of $U_{i+1}$ exceeding $U_i$ directly. We provide a method to determine if a given 'cyclic' or nontransitive' n-tuple can be realized and apply it to identify the maximum and minimum possible values for the parameters establishing the intervariable relationships, and the corresponding maximum and minimum sizes of sets that contain cyclic and nontransitive n-tuples.

Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance at a relatively low computational cost. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great potential in upgrading the quality of low-dose images without needing matched high-dose images as reference data. However, the use of two neural network generators in this approach effectively allows for different data-to-data and low-dose-to-high-dose mappings but requires a complicated reverse cycle for the data transformation, which can be both redundant and inefficient. In response to these limitations, we have developed a new cycleGAN variant based a single, adaptable generator that incorporates pretrained low-dose-to-high-dose models with adjustable 'switches'. This novel approach not only facilitates low-dose-to-high-dose transformations of data but also enables high-dose-to-low-dose transformations of enhanced images, all while minimizing the computational demands and avoiding the need for overly complex operations such as deconvolutions. In numerical experiments, our method has demonstrated superior performance compared to the original cycleGAN and various other low-dose-to-high-dose learning methods in terms of both performance and efficiency.

Recent successes in dialog understanding tasks can be attributed to pre-training methods with contrastive learning objectives. However, most studies focus on local representation enhancement through contrasting examples, overlooking the potential for contrasting information flow across tasks in a multi-task dialog setting. We present SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained model for multi-task dialog understanding that combines contrasting scenarios from both single tasks and the broader dialog system. We expand the publicly available TDiU data with over 30,000 artificially generated contrasting dialogues by leveraging the hierarchy of a Tree-Auto-Encoder. Our experiments, conducted on the TDiU dataset and a challenging multi-task dialog benchmark, demonstrate that our model outperforms the state-of-the-art using only task and sequence-level contrasting cues, resulting in significant improvements in representation learning.

This research aims to examine the geometric makeup of an ideal fluid's spacetime 
when coupled with a torsion-forming vector field and the relationship between the 
conformal Ricci-Yamabe metric and the conformal eta-Ricci-Yamabe metric. We first 
derive conditions for the conformal Ricci-Yamabe soliton to be in a state of 
expansion, stability, or contraction. Subsequently, we establish a Laplace 
equation using the conformal eta-Ricci-Yamabe soliton when the soliton's potential 
vector field is a gradient type. Additionally, this research relates an ideal 
fluid's spacetime to a Robertson-Walker spacetime and discusses various physics 
and gravitational implications.

To study the rotational characteristics of distorted halos, we utilized the angular momentum projection method on wave functions derived from the deformed relativistic Hartree-Bogoliubov theory in continuum. Our self-consistent approach effectively accounts for interactions between single particle bound states and the continuum across ground and rotational states. By analyzing rotational states in isotopes of $^{42}$Mg and $^{44}$Mg, specifically excitation energy, configuration, and density distribution, our research demonstrates that deformed halo structures endure from intrinsic ground states to collective rotational states, particularly illustrating shape decoupling effects in rotating distorted halo nuclei.

A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks, leveraging bidirectional propagation and feature alignment to utilize information from the input video. In our research, we upgrade BasicVSR by incorporating second-order grid propagation and a deformable alignment guided by optical flow, enabling the efficient exploitation of spatial and temporal information across misaligned frames. Our enhanced model, BasicVSR++, significantly outperforms the original by achieving a notable improvement in PSNR, with only a minimal increase in computational cost. Moreover, our model exhibits versatility in video restoration tasks and achieved remarkable success in video super-resolution and compressed video enhancement challenges in NTIRE 2021, earning several top ranks, with codes and models available on MMEditing.

Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and resemble weak boson colliders beyond a few TeV, a new approach known as the Effective Vector Boson Approximation has been developed to facilitate the calculation of 2-body and 3-body processes. Nevertheless, this approach has limitations when it comes to 4-body processes and processes with final state heavy gauge bosons. In this study, we expand the E-VVA framework and present a set of codes that are based on the 2-body effective form factors by implementing a diagonalization procedure, which corrects the E-VVA accuracy, particularly for 4-body and heavy boson processes, as long as they are decayed into light particles. As a result, we can regard this as an enhanced version of the E-VVA framework, which is particularly useful for 4-body processes and processes with final state heavy gauge bosons, as long as they are decayed into light particles, which is the case for the majority of the Beyond-Standard-Model searches. In order to illustrate the enhanced accuracy of the enhanced E-VVA framework, we ran comparisons with the full calculations of muon collider Beyond-Standard-Model searches, and found the predicted cross sections to be within 10-20%, and even 5% for 4-body processes and processes with final state heavy gauge bosons.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit several downstream tasks. Model-based methods additionally benefit from
planning in a learned world model. However, when learning two or more tasks
simultaneously, the influence of task diversity on the learning process and
representation must be considered. In this study, we investigate modeling
multiple tasks at once in model-based multi-task reinforcement learning. We
demonstrate that learning intertwined tasks within a single world model often
leads to negative effects, including reduced multi-task representation
benefits and even causes the model to perform worse than single-task models.
We show that decoupling tasks by utilizing separate decoder modules within a
modular world model framework, instead results in robust performance and
significantly improves individual task outcomes compared to monolithic models.
Furthermore we prove that increasing modularity by adding more independent
modules can prevent two of the modules from interfering with a third module.
Not only does this avoids the need for pre-training, but also decoupled and
modular worlds consistently outperform single-task worlds in their respective
domains. Surprisingly, even worlds trained without access to the true task
diversity exhibit these properties. To support these findings theoretically, we
utilize tasks from the Atari benchmark and prove that catastrophic interference
can occur in model-based multi-task reinforcement learning. We back up our
claims by conducting extensive experiments.

The paper provides derivations of Li-Yau and Souplet-Zhang type estimates for the equation $u_t=\Delta_\xi p + \lambda u + A(u)$ in a complete, non-compact metric measure space with compact boundary. Furthermore, the paper includes local gradient estimates for the equation $\Delta_\xi(u^p)+\lambda u + A(u) = 0$ on complete, non-compact manifolds with compact boundary.

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques.

This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space.

When the population is not fully known in advance, sampling occurs in sequence, either individually or in batches, which are obtained sequentially. This work presents a novel algorithm that allows for sequential selection of a balanced sample. The algorithm accommodates equal and unequal inclusion probabilities and can also be applied to select spatially balanced samples when the population contains geographical coordinates. Moreover, an investigation using simulated data reveals that the proposed method surpasses alternative methods.

In robotics, calibrating an eye-in-hand camera using image information is an essential task that has been extensively researched. We investigated using artificial intelligence-based methods for this purpose by leveraging only a single color image, utilizing exclusively simulated data to train the models. Our experiments involved comparing three approaches: one method predicting the camera's positioning directly from the image, another using 2D keypoints and subsequent PnP calculations, and a third method using a specialized network to extract 3D points from the image. The methods were evaluated based on their performance in estimating the camera's orientation and positional data. Our findings indicated that while direct prediction and special network extraction were more accurate than calculating 3D points, the latter could be enhanced with higher frequency down-sampling of the image. Moreover, we discovered that direct prediction achieved the best results among all methods under these experimental conditions.

In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple images that result in the same degraded data, the goal should not just be to find one solution but to explore the entire set of plausible images, or the posterior distribution. We developed a method to sample the entire posterior distribution in inverse problems by adapting a recently introduced regularization technique called Crop-and-Replace to a variation of the conditional generative adversarial network model. Our approach outperformed recent methods in two frequently used image restoration problems: super-resolution and MRI, requiring fewer adjustments and significantly less memory.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds.

Next-generation wireless networks require exceptionally high data transfer rates that could be achieved by utilizing the Terahertz frequency band. Nevertheless, signal attenuation in this band is significant over long distances, necessitating the exploration of multi-hop routing protocols. In this paper, a novel hybrid beamforming technique for multi-hop links is presented that combines a large-scale amplitude amplitude phase shift keying pre-optimization with a smaller MIMO beam training process, thereby reducing the required pilot signals. A key contribution of this study is the introduction of a reinforcement learning-based optimization method for a cost function that balances signal attenuation and pilot consumption, and demonstrates its effectiveness through a case study drawn from real-world building dimensions, showing its feasibility and high performance through both theoretical analysis and numerical simulations.

The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+19, discovering multiple scattering screens consistently located along the line of sight. Two additional screens were added to a running database of interstellar screens in the sky, which is used to explore the properties of these screens overall. The findings indicate that the screens have an average thickness of 0.11 parsecs, an average hydrogen density of 0.19 protons per cubic centimeter, and predominantly originate in the outer regions of the galactic disk.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model, but its need to learn a detailed audio regression function across the entire signal spectrum limits its pitch control capabilities. In contrast, QPNet incorporates quasi-periodic modeling based on the Karplus-Strong (KS) string synthesis to exploit the periodic nature of harmonic sounds, using a dense network (DN) to model one period of the waveform. The DN is designed as a circular dilated convolution neural network, ensuring that the first-layer output is consistent with outputs from multiple network layers by a specific number of sample steps. We demonstrate the effectiveness of QPNet in text-to-speech (TTS) systems for both deep harmonic and non-harmonic sounds, using the Mandarin Mandarin-Mercator (M-M) TTS system as a test case. The development of the M-M system involved training data from 43 Mandarin speakers and employs a Universal Joint Pronunciation Model (UJPM) to manage dissonant sounds. The TTS system's results are evaluated using the Mandarin-Mercator Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (M-MQPW) dataset, consisting of 960 utterances from 15 selected training data and assessed using the Mandarin-Mercator

This research presents a novel annotation and correction tool for Arabic texts,
namely MADARi, catering to Standard and Dialectal varieties. MADARi offers a user-
friendly interface and efficient management capabilities for annotating and handling
a considerable volume of texts. Its key features encompass a range of morphological
annotations, such as identifying the base form of words, associated clitics, part of
speech, lemma, translation, and dialect-specific markers. To facilitate productivity,
MADARi offers a set of built-in tools, including precomputed analysis to guide
annotators, access to multiple dialects via morphological analyzers, and retrieval
of prior annotations. Additionally, MADARi enables lead annotators to supervise
projects, organize batches for annotation, and integrate the data into NLP tools and
corpora.

Planets located in the habitable zones of their host stars may experience photochemistry that impacts atmospheric composition and potentially indicates life through spectral analysis. This review focuses on photochemistry in temperate,气态巨行星 and begins with an examination of external ultraviolet radiation sources, which vary according to the stars properties and habitable zones positioning. It explores how these ultraviolet fluxes are scattered within planetary atmospheres and their temperature dependencies, as well as how atmospheric  gases absorb the scattered ultraviolet radiation. Various chemical reactions, both simple and complex, are analyzed in detail, highlighting their impact on atmospheric composition. It also investigates possible photochemistry in high-entropy worlds and the effects of particle particle collisions on atmospheric chemistry. Finally, it characterizes exoplanet atmospheres through spectral analysis and presents future research directions.

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our method involves swapping the normal lead in tunneling spectroscopy with a high-resistance lead (characterized by large Ohm values). The increased resistance in this setup significantly alters tunneling conductance, impacting it in distinct ways. While the Majorana peak persists in rising as temperatures decrease in proportion to T^(2r-1), with r defined as the exponential constant in the density of states of a topological superconductor, a peak resulting from the Kondo effect in a quantum dot will behave differently, displaying an opposite trend in temperature dependence. Furthermore, we developed a model based on a clean superconductor and found that its simulated results for the majorana peak's behavior align with the predicted (1/rT) behavior, with a possible explanation for the (1/T) trend.

The development of advanced detection algorithms through deep learning has accelerated the identification of road issues, including automatic defect detection and marking analysis. To expedite and reduce costs associated with manual inspections, a comprehensive system called RoadAtlas has been developed, providing a holistic solution encompassing road flaw detection, marking parsing, interactive data visualization through a web interface, and a robust database framework supported by API tools.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence.

Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources with explicit bounding box markings. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale, size, and category diversity, consisting of 5,000 videos spanning over 200 categories. Notably, it differs from Flickr SoundNet in that it is based on video data. Our algorithm also demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on this new dataset when compared to several baseline methods.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces reparameterization techniques for convolution and multiplication operations. Moreover, it demonstrates enhanced performance on transductive and inductive node classification tasks compared to existing hyperbolic GCNs and traditional Euclidean GCNs.

This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate.

A new method has been created that successfully transfers squeezed states into stable states in optomechanical systems. The method builds upon the concept of optomechanical interactions, utilizing a three-level atom to achieve this in a setting where light and sound waves interact. By carefully selecting the system's settings, we found that a squeezed optical state can be efficiently transferred to a mechanical mode, maintaining its coherence for an extended period. Our model demonstrates the potential of this method even in situations involving significant environmental interference, thus providing a feasible pathway for applying optimized squeezed states in quantum memory applications.

We examine an expansion of modal $\mu$-calculus, specifically considering its application to sets comprised of fundamental elements. Our research also explores the properties of this research in terms of simulation, bisimulation, and model checking.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and
these variations have significant implications for decision-making, as well as
mathematical applications, including delay-period scaling, intertemporal choice,
hyperbolic discounting, and the hot/cold system model.

When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity theory with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.

A signed graph is created by adding a polarity to the edges of an existing graph, and this concept of signed graphs has recently been incorporated into the study of graph theory for various representations and mapping purposes. Mapping restrictions on signed graphs are subject to investigation, and a recent study explores the representation and mapping limitations of certain signed graphs that are constructed based on their 'Double Covers'. This construction method is bounded by certain properties, and it is examined whether these bounds can be influenced by considering graphs with specific cyclic patterns and properties.

For a class of quadratic Hamiltonians, a transformation of Weyl-Wigner symbols through a change of variables reveals the canonical thermal equilibrium quantum states, using the Weyl-Wigner representations and metaplectic operators, whose associated unitary classical structures behave predictably under the transformation, exposing the complex symplectic matrix that dictates the entire thermal equilibrium state and thereby determines its thermal properties. Additionally, a thorough examination is performed of four distinct types of Hamiltonian dynamics: parabolic, elliptic, hyperbolic, and loxodromic dynamics. Semiclassical and high-temperature approximations are both determined and contrasted to their respective classical or quadratic behaviors.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, as demonstrated by Rashid et al. in their recent experiments, and can be modeled using the two-level system with interactions akin to those in -a Mott insulator. Within this framework, such temperatures can be interpreted as scenarios where high-energy states possess greater population than low-energy states. Nonetheless, it is crucial to acknowledge that the equilibrium between two levels is achievable only when the system is isolated, and the distribution of states in such isolated systems, particularly within a global two-level model, may not always adhere to a single temperature. Consequently, until further studies are conducted and data is gathered, drawing conclusions about heat and work in these systems would be premature.

Let G be an abelian group and A a nonempty subset of G, with elements indexed as $a_0, a_1,..., a_{k-1}$. For any positive integer h less than or equal to k, we can calculate a restricted signed sumset denoted as $h\hat{}_{\underline{+}}A$, which comprises sums of $a_i$ with weights from {-1,0,1}. The goal of this article is to solve the minimum value of $|h\hat{}_{\underline{+}}A|$, where $|A|$, when A is a set of integers, and investigate the underlying structure of A to achieve this minimum value. Additionally, some open questions related to $h\hat{}_{\underline{+}}A$ are also presented in this article.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for malignancy and dysplasia using histological analysis. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved medical pattern recognition accuracy; however, training these models necessitates vast collections of annotated medical images. In this context, we're presenting UniToPatho, a comprehensive dataset consisting of 9536 annotated H&E stained patches derived from 292 whole-slide images, designed for deep learning-based classification and grading of colorectal polyps and adenomas. This dataset will facilitate the development and testing of deep learning models aimed at enhancing computational assistance in pathology diagnosis.

A novel numerical approach has been introduced for solving time-harmonic acoustic scattering issues, primarily centered around analyzing the impact of smoothly varying material inhomogeneities on plane waves. This method's efficiency is optimal for high-frequency scenarios and is adaptable across any given frequency $\omega$. The approach operates within a time-domain framework, consisting of three main components: generating a suitable incoming plane wave with compact support, transforming this solution into the frequency domain through deconvolution, and finally computing the scattered field using a high-frequency adaptive algorithm based on the boundary element method. Notably, the approach leverages the existing code for scattering problems with a point source, thereby reutilizing much of the computational work already done. The code is implemented in C++ and integrated with the BEMIS software package for time-domain boundary element methods. A theoretical analysis supporting the approach, along with several practical examples demonstrating its effectiveness, are provided in the accompanying paper.

We analyzed the isotopic ratios of hydrogen in water extracted from the Chelyabinsk and Benenitra meteorites, discovering significant variations. The water isotopic ratios in both meteors cover a wide range, spanning 4.5 DBE to 1000+ DBE, with the latter being found in apatites from Benenitra. The chondrules within these meteorites contained moderate到高 levels of hydrogen isotopes (0.4-4.0 DBE). Notably, the diverse water isotopic findings in these meteorites suggest that the building blocks of the early inner solar system, such as chondrules and mesostases, exhibited distinct hydrogen isotopic characteristics, likely attributed to wet accretion.

Using the algebraic Bethe-ansatz method, we find exact expressions for scalar products and form factors of higher-spin XXZ chains. This applies to any spin values and mixtures thereof. We verify the affine quantum-group symmetry, $U_q(\hat{sl_2})$, for the XXZ chain's monodromy matrix, enabling exact derivation. Specifically, we use quantum-group symmetry to explicitly obtain diagonalized forms for the B and C operators within the F-basis of the spin-1/2 XXZ chain. This achievement substantiates prior conjectures about the algebraic Bethe-ansatz's correlation function calculations. These results provide a crucial foundation for systematic studies of form factors and correlation functions across solvable models connected to integrable XXZ spin chains.

Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Conventional two-stage speech-to-text translation systems, which convert speech to the source language and then translate to the target language, have inherent flaws. They are prone to propagating errors from the first stage and require substantial data for both languages. We present a novel, direct translation system that bypasses the need for speech-to-text data for the source language. Our model combines an end-to-end speech-to-text translation system and a speech-to-text translation model for the source language. It leverages transfer learning to translate the speech. Our results demonstrate a significant performance improvement, achieving a 1-dB reduction in total mean squared error over the baseline system.

We assess the applicability of three different methods for calculating electromagnetic multipoles: Cartesian primitive multipoles, irreducible multipoles and spherical multipoles. Our findings suggest that the spherical multipoles provide the most accurate description of electromagnetic scattering behavior, as demonstrated with an example of an amorphous silicon sphere. These multipoles are utilized to model the optical force exerted on particles composed of semiconductors, dielectrics, and metals over a broad range of wavelengths spanning from the dipolar regime down to the Mie regime.

This study introduces two categories of elements in the algebra U(gl(n)), specifically double Young-Capelli bitableaux and central Schur elements, both exhibiting remarkable action on the highest weight vectors of irreducible Schur modules. The central Schur elements can be viewed as a sum of double Young-Capelli bitableaux corresponding to various strictly increasing Young tableaux. These elements equate to preimages under the Harish-Chandra isomorphism of shifted Schur polynomials, aligning with quantum immanants as per Okounkov. Notably, the representation of Harish-Chandra images for the Young-Capelli bitableaux on U(sl(m,C)) is an irreducible Schur module.

Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we examine the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino characteristics, and dark matter behavior. By integrating the type-II seesaw mechanism with a minimal dark sector, we establish theoretical constraints on the model's parameters, analyzing the stability of the vacuum and dark matter's WIMP behavior. We determine the model's impact on the Higgs potential, identifying the minimum viable neutrino mass generated through the type-II seesaw mechanism. Furthermore, we identify the allowed dark matter mass range to maintain WIMP-like behavior and satisfy dark matter density observations. We also investigate the decays of a specific scalar particle that could be detected in future experiments, with the model's ability to be tested at both the LHC and future colliders such as the FCC-ee and CEPC.

We have developed a general model to describe the electron orbital interactions and configurations of 4d and 5d transition metals. Our approach employs a Heisenberg-Hamiltonian with terms that account for electron orbital interactions, based on a quasiparticle approach in conjunction with a Löwdin method to expand the one-electron quasiparticle Hamiltonian to a many-electron Hamillonian. The resulting model reveals the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ electrons in 4d and 5d metals to be significantly influential in determining electron orbital configurations, with our findings supported by detailed explanations using a case study of RuO$_2$.

This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW.

Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020, and the corresponding presentation can be found at the provided URL.

ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data, encompassing
elementary to complex methodologies.

Evaluating Newtonian potentials over complex two-dimensional regions efficiently and accurately is crucial for solving Poisson's equation. While the authors provide a straightforward and effective algorithm specifically designed for this purpose, it notably avoids any scaling issues when dealing with large objects, such as in astrophysical simulations, where the method can be accurately and efficiently implemented using a parallel version based on an algorithm called Fast Multipole Method.
